Only then turn the heat on.
steps.note: This is how every professional kitchen in the world works and it is why they are calm. Cooking is easy once the chopping is behind you.

steps.test: Make beans on toast with both parts ready at the same moment.
how: Work backwards: the toast takes two minutes, the beans take four. Beans first.
Butter on the plate and the table set before either is ready.
Hot food on a warm plate.
steps.note: The humblest possible lesson in timing two things, and it is exactly the same skill as getting a roast and its vegetables to land together.

steps.test: Cook pasta and a sauce and get them together hot.
how: Sauce on first, pasta into properly salted boiling water second.
Taste the pasta a minute before the packet says.
Drain, then straight into the sauce pan and toss — never sauce sitting on top.
steps.note: Salting the water and finishing the pasta in the sauce are the two things that separate a decent plate of pasta from a sad one, and both are free.

steps.test: Fry something without burning it or leaving it raw.
how: Pan properly hot before anything goes in — a drop of water should dance.
Do not crowd the pan. Two batches beats one steamed mess.
Leave it alone. Turn it once, when it lets go of the pan by itself.
steps.note: Turning things over and over is the commonest mistake there is. A thing that is stuck is not ready to turn; when it is ready, it releases.

steps.test: Taste as you go, and change it — more salt, or something sharp.
how: Taste before it goes on the plate, every single time.
Flat and dull usually means salt. Heavy and rich usually means something sharp: lemon, vinegar, mustard.
Add a little, stir, taste again.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes you a cook rather than a recipe follower. Nobody can taste your food from a page in a book.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for yourself, start to finish.
how: Something real: meat or fish or eggs, a vegetable, something to cook it in.
Everything ready first, taste before serving, sit down to eat it.
Clear the kitchen afterwards.
steps.note: A whole meal on your own is the middle of this ladder. If this is already routine for you, cook something you have never cooked before and count that.

steps.test: Clean as you go, so the kitchen is nearly clear when you sit down.
how: Wash each thing while the next thing cooks.
Bin, cloth and hot soapy water within reach from the start.
The rung is what the kitchen looks like when the food goes on the table.
steps.note: This is the habit that decides whether cooking feels like a pleasure or a chore, and it costs no extra time at all — only different timing.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for your family.
how: Something you have cooked before rather than a first attempt.
Ask beforehand what nobody will eat, so you are not surprised.
Plates warm, everything landing together, table laid.
steps.note: Feeding people is the oldest way there is of saying something you might not say out loud. This rung is worth more than the four above it.

steps.test: Cook the same meal again, better.
how: Write down one thing you would change before you forget it.
Cook it again within a fortnight with that one change.
Ask whether they noticed.
steps.note: Cooking the same thing three times beats cooking three different things. The second and third times are where the skill actually appears.

steps.test: Time three things so they are all ready together.
how: Write the times backwards from when you want to eat.
The longest thing goes on first. Everything else fits around it.
One timer per thing if you need it.
steps.note: This is the whole difficulty of cooking a meal, in one rung. Once you can do this with three things, a Christmas dinner is only the same problem with eight.

steps.test: Cook a meal out of whatever happened to be in the house.
how: Look at what you have first, then decide, rather than deciding then shopping.
Eggs, onions, a tin of something and whatever vegetable is going over is a meal.
No shopping trip allowed.
steps.note: This is where cooking starts saving you real money and real waste. It is also the skill that means you are never stuck.

steps.test: Cook for somebody who cannot eat something, and get it right.
how: Ask exactly what they cannot have, and whether it is a preference or a medical matter.
Read the labels on anything from a packet — it hides in sauces, stock and bread.
Clean board, clean pan, clean knife if it is serious.
steps.note: Being cooked for safely is rare enough that people remember who did it. Take it seriously and ask rather than assuming.

steps.test: Cook a roast, with the vegetables, all ready together.
how: Work backwards from the time you want to eat, on paper.
Meat rests for fifteen or twenty minutes — that is when the vegetables finish and the gravy happens.
A cheap cut cooked slowly beats an expensive one cooked badly.
steps.note: The roast is the traditional test and it deserves its reputation: six things, one oven, one moment. The resting time is the trick that makes it possible.

steps.test: Cook three courses and get them all to the table hot.
how: Pudding made first and left. Starter prepared cold or nearly cooked.
Main the only thing actually happening while people are in the house.
Written plan on the worktop.
steps.note: Doing the work in advance is the whole answer. Three courses is not three times the cooking, it is one course cooked while people are there and two done that morning.

steps.test: Cook a meal for eight people.
how: Choose something that scales and waits: a stew, a curry, a big tray bake, a pot of soup and good bread.
Cook it the day before if you can — most of these are better for it.
Count the plates, forks and chairs before the day.
steps.note: Numbers are not the hard part. Choosing a dish that forgives being held for half an hour is the whole skill of cooking for a crowd.

steps.test: Cook for the whole group at a day out.
how: A big pot of something, or a fire and something to grill, or a proper picnic you actually made.
Plan for it being cold, wet, and later than intended.
Bring more than you think, and something hot to drink.
steps.note: Feeding people outdoors is the oldest version of this and the one nobody forgets. It is also the end of the ladder: you can now feed anybody, anywhere.

tracks.about: Being able to feed yourself and other people well, from real ingredients, without a recipe in your hand. This is the most immediately useful ladder in the school: it saves real money every week, it is the practical half of Real food, and a person who can cook is welcome everywhere. It goes from boiling an egg to a roast and three courses, in about three months of cooking a few times a week — which you were going to do anyway.

tracks.name: Baking
tracks.line: From weighing accurately to a loaf of your own, and selling what you made.

steps.test: Weigh five things accurately on a scale, to the gram.
how: Bowl on the scale, zero it, then add. Zero it again for the next thing.
Get it exact rather than close. Baking is the one place where close is not good enough.
No scale? Kitchen scales are cheap second hand and most charity shops have one.
steps.note: Cooking forgives, baking does not. Everything above this rung depends on the weighing being honest.

steps.test: Bake something from a packet mix, exactly as it says.
how: Read it all the way through first. Then follow it to the letter.
Oven on early — it takes fifteen minutes to get properly hot.
Set a timer and check five minutes before it goes off.
steps.note: A packet mix takes all the decisions away so that you learn the oven, the tin and the timing without anything else to go wrong.

steps.test: Line and grease a tin so nothing sticks.
how: Butter the tin, then a circle of baking paper in the bottom, then butter that too.
For a loaf tin, a long strip up and over both ends acts as handles.
No paper? Butter and a dusting of flour, tapped out.
steps.note: More home baking is ruined at the turning-out stage than at any other. Two minutes of lining saves the whole thing.

steps.test: Bake something by following a written recipe on your own.
how: Everything weighed and lined up before you start.
Follow it exactly, even the bits you would change.
Write on the recipe afterwards what you noticed.
steps.note: Follow it exactly once before you ever improvise. You cannot tell what a change did unless you know what the original does.

steps.test: Rub butter into flour until it looks like breadcrumbs.
how: Cold butter, cut into small cubes, straight from the fridge.
Fingertips only, lifting the mixture up and letting it fall as you rub.
Stop when it looks like coarse breadcrumbs — a few bigger lumps are fine.
steps.note: Cold hands and cold butter. This one technique is the base of scones, shortbread, crumble and pastry, so it is worth ten minutes of practice.

steps.test: Make scones or shortbread that come out right.
how: Handle the dough as little as possible — the less you work it the lighter it is.
Hot oven, high shelf, and do not open the door for the first ten minutes.
Cut straight down with the cutter, no twisting, or they rise crooked.
steps.note: The first thing you will make that people ask for again. It is also the quickest: twenty minutes from a cold kitchen to something on a plate.

steps.test: Know when something is done without cutting it open.
how: A skewer into the middle comes out clean. A sponge springs back when pressed.
Bread sounds hollow when you knock the bottom of it.
Colour first, then the test. Pale means underdone whatever the timer says.
steps.note: Ovens all lie by ten or twenty degrees. Learning the tests rather than trusting the timer is what makes your baking work in anybody's kitchen.

steps.test: Bake a sponge that rises.
how: Butter and sugar beaten until genuinely pale and fluffy — a good five minutes.
Eggs added a little at a time so it does not split.
Flour folded in gently at the end. Beating here knocks the air out.
steps.note: A risen sponge is air, and the air went in during the beating. This is the rung that teaches why a method is in the order it is in.

steps.test: Bake something twice, and make the second one better.
how: Write down one change before you forget: five minutes less, a little more salt, a hotter oven.
Same recipe, one change only, within a fortnight.
Note which was better.
steps.note: One change at a time is the only way to learn anything from your own baking. Two changes and you will never know which did it.

steps.test: Make a dough and knead it for ten full minutes.
how: Timer on. Ten minutes is much longer than it feels — most people stop at three.
Push it away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter, repeat.
It goes from a shaggy lump to smooth and springy. That change is what you are looking for.
steps.note: Kneading is the whole of bread and there is no shortcut worth having. Ten minutes of it is also a remarkably good way to be in a bad mood less.

steps.test: Make a loaf of bread from flour, water, salt and yeast.
how: Four ingredients only. Nothing else belongs in a loaf.
Knead ten minutes, rise until doubled, knock back, shape, rise again, bake hot.
It costs very little and takes fifteen minutes of actual work spread over an afternoon.
steps.note: A shop loaf has a label with twenty things on it. Yours has four. This one rung is the whole argument of Real food, made edible.

steps.test: Make a loaf where the crumb is even all the way through.
how: Knock the air out properly before the second rise, and shape it tightly.
Do not let the second rise go too far — it should spring back slowly when pressed.
Cut it only when it is cool, however hard that is.
steps.note: Big holes at the top and dense at the bottom is the classic second loaf. Proper shaping and not over-proving is the fix.

steps.test: Bake something with a filling that does not leak.
how: Cold pastry, cold filling, and seal the edges with a wet finger and a fork.
Cut a hole or two in the top so the steam has a way out.
Do not overfill. Everybody overfills.
steps.note: Leaks come from steam with nowhere to go. A couple of slits in the lid is the difference between a pie and a tray to scrub.

steps.test: Ice or decorate something so it looks like it was meant to.
how: Completely cold before any icing goes near it, or it slides off.
A thin first coat to catch the crumbs, then the real coat on top.
Simple and neat beats elaborate and messy every time.
steps.note: Looking deliberate is mostly patience: cold cake, thin first coat, one colour done neatly. It doubles the pleasure for the person receiving it.

steps.test: Bake something without looking at the recipe.
how: Pick the thing you have made most often.
Write the recipe out from memory first, then bake it and check.
Whatever you got wrong is the bit you never actually learned.
steps.note: Having one thing in your head that you can make in anybody's kitchen with no book is worth more than twenty recipes you can follow.

steps.test: Bake for somebody's birthday.
how: Ask what they actually like rather than baking what you like making.
Make it the day before so you are not rushing.
Bake a small test version first if it is a new one.
steps.note: A baked thing made by a person is one of the few gifts nobody has ever had too many of, and it costs very little.

steps.test: Work out what a batch costs you to make.
how: Weigh the flour, butter, sugar and eggs you used and price each from the receipt.
Add something for the electricity and the paper.
Divide by the number of pieces.
steps.note: This is where baking meets Money and value, and the numbers usually surprise people in both directions. You cannot price anything until you know this.

steps.test: Bake to order for somebody else, to exactly what they asked for.
how: Write down what they asked for and read it back to them.
Agree the day and the time before you agree anything else.
Deliver it when you said, not when it is convenient.
steps.note: Somebody else's specification is a different job from your own baking. Getting the brief right, and on time, is most of what being paid for anything is.

steps.test: Price what you baked and sell it to people who are not related to you.
how: Cost plus your time, then a real price, written on a card.
A stall, a second-hand sale, a school fair, a sign at the gate, a message to the street group.
Say the price out loud without apologising for it.
steps.note: The nerve is not in the baking, it is in saying the number. That is the rung. Money earned from something you made changes how you see your own hands.

steps.test: Teach somebody to bake one thing, start to finish, hands off.
how: Your hands behind your back. Say it, do not do it.
Let them make the mistakes — the crooked scones teach more than your perfect ones.
They take the whole batch home.
steps.note: Hands off is the hard part and the whole rung. Something somebody made themselves, badly, with you beside them, is what makes them a baker.

tracks.about: Baking is chemistry that you get to eat, and unlike cooking it rewards exactness rather than judgement, which makes it the better one to learn with children. The ladder goes from a packet mix to a proper loaf of bread from flour, water and salt — which costs very little and beats anything in a shop — and ends by selling what you made to somebody who is not related to you, which is a different kind of nerve entirely.

tracks.name: Cooking on fire
tracks.line: Toast on a stick to a whole meal outdoors.

steps.test: Toast something on a stick over a fire and eat it.
Wait for embers instead of cooking on flames.
steps.note: Flames burn the outside and leave the middle raw. Embers are what you actually cook on.

steps.test: Cook an egg or a sausage over a fire without burning it.
Bake a bread twist on a stick.
Wrap something in foil and cook it in the embers.
Keep a fire steady at cooking heat for twenty minutes.
Cook a one-pot meal over a fire for two people.
Set up a pot so it hangs or stands steady over the heat.
Cook two things at once over the same fire.
Wash up outdoors and leave no trace of any of it.
Cook a full meal outdoors for six.
Run the fire and the food for a whole day out.

tracks.name: Growing
tracks.line: One seed to feeding people.

steps.test: Plant a seed and keep it alive for a month.
Water it without drowning it, and say how you knew.
Grow something fast — cress, radishes — and eat it.
Grow something you then eat, that took longer than a month.
Find out what your soil is like and what suits it.
Dig a bed or fill a pot properly and plant it out.
Sow seed in a tray and prick the seedlings out.
Keep a patch weeded every week for a month.
Lose a crop, work out why, and say what you would do differently.
steps.note: Everybody who grows anything kills things. The ones who get good are the ones who work out why.

steps.test: Grow three different things through a whole season.
Harvest something at the right moment, not too early or too late.
Grow something from a cutting rather than a seed.
Make compost and put it back on the ground.
Grow something over winter.
Save seed and grow next year's from it.
Grow enough of one thing to make a whole meal from it.
Grow enough to give some away.
Keep a note through a season of what worked and what did not.
Plant something that will not be ready for a year.
Run a growing patch for the group.

tracks.name: Keeping food
tracks.line: Jam to a full store cupboard.

steps.test: Make jam that sets.
Sterilise the jars properly before you fill them.
Label and date everything you put away.
Make a second batch that sets better than the first.
Pickle something in vinegar.
Eat it a month later and say whether it worked.
Freeze a harvest so it is still good in three months.
Dry herbs or fruit until they keep.
Make a chutney.
Ferment something — sauerkraut, kefir, a sourdough starter.
Keep a starter or a ferment alive for a month.
Salt or cure something.
Bake with something you preserved yourself.
Cook a whole meal using three things you put away.
Preserve a glut that would otherwise have been thrown out.
Fill a shelf with things you made that keep.
Know which of them is safe how long, and why.
Throw out something that went wrong, without arguing with yourself.
Give away a box of it and have people ask for more.
Teach somebody to make one thing that keeps.

tracks.name: Feeding people
tracks.line: From laying the table properly, to hosting a meal with a reason to it for eight or more people.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child hosts with a grown-up
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child can lay, serve and host beside a grown-up, and the grown-up looks after the hot cooking. It starts at your own table (laying it, serving others first, asking what people like), moves to inviting one guest and planning the meal on paper with the timings worked backwards, and then to bigger tables and guests who have never met. It ends with a meal for eight or more with a reason to it, such as a birthday or a welcome. The food can be simple; this ladder is about the table and the people round it, and the cooking ladder (Cooking a meal) is where the cooking itself is learned.

steps.test: Lay the table for the next meal at home: a plate, a knife and fork or spoon, a glass and a napkin at every place.
steps.note: Fork on the left, knife on the right with the blade facing the plate, glass above the knife. A folded square of kitchen roll is a fine napkin. If your household eats in another way, such as with hands or chopsticks, lay it properly in that way. If you already lay it every day, do it on purpose tonight and count it.

steps.test: At the next meal, pour everybody's water before your own, and sit down last.
steps.note: A jug of tap water on the table makes it easy. Look round before you sit: has everybody got a plate, a drink and what they need? Then sit.

steps.test: At a meal, notice what somebody needs before they ask, and pass it to them.
steps.note: The salt, the bread, the sauce, a spoon for the little one. Keep half an eye on the table while you eat. Once is enough for the rung, and you will find yourself doing it again.

steps.test: Ask everybody at home what meal they would most like this week, and what they do not like or cannot eat.
steps.note: Write the answers down. Then help to make one of the favourites happen this week, even if all you do is ask for it on the shopping list. This is the same question you will ask guests later.

steps.test: Put one thing on the table that nobody asked for.
steps.note: A jug of flowers or leaves from outside, a folded napkin at each place, a small bowl of lemon slices for the water. A candle is lovely, lit by a grown-up and kept away from sleeves. A table with something on it tells guests they were expected, and it need cost nothing.

steps.test: Invite one person who does not live with you to a meal at home, and ask what they cannot or do not eat.
steps.note: A friend, a neighbour, a grandparent, a colleague. "Would you come for a meal on Friday? Is there anything you do not eat?" Write the answer down. A child invites with a grown-up's say-so, and a friend's parent gets asked too.

steps.test: Plan that meal on paper: what you will serve, what is already in the house, and what you still need.
steps.note: Keep it simple: one main dish, something green, something sweet or some fruit. Choose food you have made before. Cross off what you already have; the shopping list is what is left. A soup and bread is a proper meal.

steps.test: Write the timings backwards from the moment you want to sit down.
steps.note: Sitting down at 6:30? The pasta goes in at 6:15, the water on at 6:00, the table is laid at 5:45, the pudding is made at 5:00. Start from the plates on the table and work back. Everything else is guessing.

steps.test: Make one part of the meal the day before, so there is less to do on the day.
steps.note: A soup, a stew, a pudding, a salad dressing, a batch of biscuits. Most soups and stews taste as good or better the next day. Keep it in the fridge, covered.

steps.test: Host the meal: greet your guest at the door, sit down within ten minutes of the time you planned, and eat with them.
steps.note: Follow your backwards timings. Once the food is on the table, stay sitting; the washing up can wait. If something goes wrong, such as a burnt edge or a runny sauce, serve it with a smile and do not apologise more than once.

steps.test: The day after, write down three things that went well and one thing to do differently next time.
steps.note: Was the timing right? Did you get to sit down? Was there too much food, or too little? Keep the note with your plan; it is the start of your own way of hosting.

steps.test: Host a meal for three or four guests who do not all know each other, and introduce each one with something they share.
steps.note: "Ana, this is Joe. You both walk by the river every morning." Plan it with the same paper plan and backwards timings. If you hosted two or three people in Meeting people, part two, this time the meal itself is planned and cooked.

steps.test: During a meal, bring the quietest guest into the talk with one question that suits them.
steps.note: Something you already know they enjoy: "Joe, how is the vegetable patch doing?" Then let them answer fully before anybody else speaks. Watch for them again later in the evening.

steps.test: Let a guest help with one job, and let them do it their way.
steps.note: Carrying plates, filling glasses, cutting the bread. Most people like to help and feel more at home when they do. Say thank you, and do not redo it after them.

steps.test: Invite somebody round on the same day and feed them from what is already in the house.
steps.note: Pasta with a tin of tomatoes and an onion, eggs on toast, a pan of soup from the vegetables in the fridge. No shopping allowed. Tell them it is simple; it is the being asked that people remember.

steps.test: Host a meal for six that costs no more than your household's food for a normal day.
steps.note: Beans, lentils, rice, potatoes, pasta, eggs and seasonal vegetables go a long way. Or ask each guest to bring one dish so the table is shared. Keep the receipt and add it up afterwards.

steps.test: Plan a meal for eight or more with a reason to it, and send the invitations two weeks ahead.
steps.note: A birthday, a welcome for somebody new, a leaving, a finished exam, the first evening of a season. Say the reason in the invitation and ask what people do not eat. Paper plan, backwards timings and a day-before dish, as before. A child plans this with a grown-up.

steps.test: Host that meal for eight or more, sit down with your guests, and send everybody home with something.
steps.note: A slice of cake wrapped in a napkin, a jar of soup, a cutting from a plant, a photo from the evening sent the next day. Borrow chairs and plates if you need to, or eat on blankets outside in good weather. This is the far end of the ladder.

tracks.name: In the kitchen
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Hands washed, then stirring, spreading, cracking and making.

steps.test: Wash your hands properly before you touch any food.
how: Warm water, soap, and long enough to sing something short.
Backs of the hands and between the fingers, not just the palms.
Dry them on a towel, not on your clothes.
steps.note: Start every single session with this and it becomes automatic within a fortnight. Do it yourself beside them rather than telling them to.

steps.test: Put an apron on by yourself.
how: Over the head first, then the ties.
A tea towel tucked in at the neck works perfectly well as an apron.
Let them struggle with the ties for a while before you help.
steps.note: The apron is the signal that this is a proper job, not playing. Children take the whole session more seriously with one on.

steps.test: Stir something in a bowl until it is all mixed and nothing is left at the bottom.
how: A big bowl on a damp cloth so it does not spin.
Show them how to go round the bottom edge where it hides.
Let them check by lifting the spoon and looking.
steps.note: Give them the checking as well as the stirring. A child who has been shown how to tell when a job is done will do it properly without being watched.

steps.test: Pour from a small jug into a bowl without spilling it.
how: Small jug, half full. Both hands.
Slow and close — hold the jug low, near the bowl.
Practise with water at the sink first, where spills do not matter.
steps.note: Practising with water first is the trick for all of this. Ten free goes at the sink is worth more than one careful go with the eggs.

steps.test: Spread butter on a slice of bread, right to the edges, without tearing it.
how: Soft butter, left out beforehand. Hard butter tears the bread and they get cross.
A round-ended knife, spreading from the middle outwards.
Look at the corners together at the end.
steps.note: The corners are the standard, and it is a standard a four-year-old can see for themselves. That is what makes it a good first job.

steps.test: Peel a banana or a satsuma all by yourself.
how: Start the satsuma peel for them with your thumbnail, then hands off.
A banana opens more easily from the bottom than the stalk end.
Their fruit to eat afterwards.
steps.note: Let them finish it even when it takes three minutes and makes a mess. Finishing it themselves is the entire rung.

steps.test: Crack an egg into a bowl.
how: Tap it firmly on the flat worktop, not on the edge of the bowl — it shatters less.
Both thumbs in the crack, open it over the bowl.
Use a separate small bowl so a bad one does not spoil the mixture.
steps.note: The small bowl is how you let them do it without any risk to the meal, which means you can say yes rather than 'not this time'.

steps.test: Pick the bits of shell out.
how: A bigger piece of shell picks up a small one far more easily than fingers do.
Look properly rather than quickly.
Their job to say when it is clear.
steps.note: Fixing your own mistake without anybody being cross about it is a small, important lesson, and this is the safest possible place to learn it.

steps.test: Weigh something on the scales and say the number out loud.
how: Bowl on, zero it together, then spoon it in slowly.
Let them stop at the right number rather than you saying stop.
Numbers on a scale are real numbers doing a real job.
steps.note: This is reading, counting and a bit of chemistry, and none of it feels like a lesson. It is also the first rung of the Baking ladder.

steps.test: Make a sandwich and give it to somebody to eat.
how: Their choice of filling, within reason.
Cut it however they think is best.
They carry it and hand it over themselves.
steps.note: The handing-over is the important half. Making something that another person actually eats is the first time a child feeds somebody, and they know it.

steps.test: Wipe the table and put your things in the sink afterwards.
how: Damp cloth, and show them the crumbs they missed rather than doing it after them.
Everything they used goes in the sink or the dishwasher.
Apron off and hung up last.
steps.note: Clearing up is part of the job, not a punishment at the end of it. Start it at four and it is never a battle at fourteen.

steps.test: Help make one whole thing for everybody's tea.
how: Pick something with jobs they can genuinely do: a tray bake, a crumble, soup, buns.
Tell everybody at the table who made it.
Let them serve it out.
steps.note: Say their name out loud when the food goes on the table. Being useful to the whole family, publicly, is what they are actually after.

tracks.about: For a child of about four and upwards, with a grown-up beside them. Children want to be in the kitchen long before we let them, and a four-year-old can genuinely stir, pour, peel a satsuma, crack an egg and make a sandwich for somebody else. Every rung here is a real job that actually needed doing, which is the whole point: children can tell the difference between helping and being given something to keep them busy.

categories.name: Money and business
categories.line: Handling it, earning it, selling, running something, investing.

tracks.name: Money and value, part one
tracks.line: From writing down what you spend to being paid three times for one thing.

steps.test: Write down every penny you spend today.
steps.note: On paper or the notes app. No changing anything; just seeing it.

steps.test: Write down, roughly, what came in this month and what went out.
steps.note: One page. Two numbers and the gap between them is more than most people ever look at.

steps.test: Name three things you own that somebody would pay for.
steps.note: Not the house. A bike, a coat, a tool, a book, a game. Write a price beside each.

steps.test: Sell one thing you no longer need, for any price.
steps.note: An online listing, a second-hand sale, a friend. Given away does not count; any price does. The point is asking for money and getting it.

steps.test: Ask for a better price on one thing, politely.
steps.note: "Is that your best price?" at a market, on a phone contract, on anything second-hand. A no costs nothing.

steps.test: Cancel one thing you pay for and do not use.
steps.note: A subscription, a membership, a service. If there is nothing to cancel, count it and enjoy that.

steps.test: Write down one skill you have that somebody would pay for.
steps.note: Everybody has one. Tidying, driving, baking, explaining a phone, fixing a bike, minding a dog. Write it as an offer: "I can … for …".

steps.test: Make one thing that could be sold.
steps.note: A card, a loaf, a poster, a small repair, a jar of something. Made, finished, and you would take money for it.

steps.test: Offer one thing to one person for money.
steps.note: An hour of help, a bake, a lift, a lesson. A no is a fine answer; the rung is the offer, said out loud.

steps.test: Earn some money you did not have this morning, however small.
steps.note: Any honest way. Most people go years without earning anything outside their job.

steps.test: Find out properly what three people you know do for a living.
steps.note: What they actually do all day, what is hard, what pays. Ask; people like being asked.

steps.test: Set one money goal with a number and a date, written down.
steps.note: "200 by the end of next month, from things I make or do." Small and real beats big and vague.

steps.test: Put aside a tenth of anything that comes in this week, before you spend.
steps.note: A jar, a separate account, an envelope. The oldest money habit there is. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done.

steps.test: Ask for something you want at work or in a deal: more, better, or sooner.
steps.note: A day off, a rate, a discount, a start date. Ask once, plainly, then stop talking.

steps.test: Price one thing you could sell, from what it costs you to what people pay.
steps.note: Materials, time, what the shop charges. Write the number down and say it out loud without flinching.

steps.test: Sell that thing three times.
steps.note: Three different people, or the same one thrice. Now you know it sells.

steps.test: Read one book, or listen to one long talk, by somebody who has actually made money.
steps.note: Not a guru: a person who built and ran something. One, all the way through.

steps.test: Spend nothing for one whole day.
steps.note: Not a penny. Notice how often the hand goes to the pocket. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done.

steps.test: Write a one-page plan for something you could run.
steps.note: What it is, who it is for, what it costs, what it earns, what you would do first. One page, no more.

steps.test: Get paid by three different people for the same thing.
steps.note: That is a business, however small. Part two grows it.

tracks.about: Money made and money kept, in twenty rungs that start with writing down what you spent today and end with three different people paying you for the same thing. Selling one thing, asking for a better price, an offer said out loud, a tenth put aside. Small, real, and most of it is nerve rather than knowledge.

tracks.name: Handling money
tracks.line: From putting the coins in order to doing a whole week's shop under budget, receipt checked.
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child with pocket money and a grown-up can climb it side by side. For a child it is the real basics, coins, change and value; a grown-up does the same rungs faster, and the notes say what the grown-up version looks like. It goes from coins in order, to change in your head, to price per gram on the shelf, to a week of money written down, and ends with a whole week's shop planned on paper and done under budget. None of it needs any money beyond what the household already spends.

steps.test: Put one of each coin on the table and put them in order of value, smallest first.
steps.note: Every coin your country uses, from the smallest to the largest. A child names each one out loud. No coins in the house: your central bank or mint shows pictures of them online. Already easy? Tip out a purse or a jar of mixed coins and total it in your head, then count to check.

steps.test: Make one whole unit of your money (a pound, a dollar, a euro) out of coins in three different ways.
steps.note: For example two halves, five fifths, or one half, two fifths and a tenth, in whatever coins you have. A grown-up can make 3.85 in the fewest coins possible, then in the most.

steps.test: In a shop, add up the prices of three things in your head before you reach the till.
steps.note: Round each price to the nearest tenth of a unit (10p, 10 cents) to make it easier, then check your answer against the till. No trip to a shop today: do it with a receipt from the bin or three prices on a supermarket website.

steps.test: Pay for something small with cash, and count your change before you walk away.
steps.note: Use something the house needs anyway: milk, bread, a stamp. A child hands over the money and counts the change while the grown-up waits. If it is wrong, say so politely at the counter; that is part of the rung.

steps.test: Play shop at home: one person buys, the other gives change from a 5 note, five times in a row with no mistakes.
steps.note: Real coins or paper ones. Prices under 5, like 3.40 or 1.85. Count up from the price to 5, the way shops used to. A grown-up on their own can do five from old receipts on paper.

steps.test: Work out, in your head, the change from 10 and from 20 for five different prices, and get all five right.
steps.note: Take prices from a receipt or a supermarket leaflet: 7.35 from 10 is 2.65. Write your answers first, then check on a calculator.

steps.test: Compare two sizes of the same thing on a shop shelf, using the price per 100 grams, and say which is better value.
steps.note: The smaller numbers on the shelf label give the price per 100g, per kilo or per item. Cereal, rice, washing-up liquid. No shop today: the same numbers are on a supermarket website.

steps.test: Find one thing where the bigger pack costs more per 100 grams than the smaller one.
steps.note: It happens more often than people expect, especially with offers. Write down what it was. That is the reason to read the price per 100g line every time.

steps.test: Check every card or phone payment from the last seven days against what you remember buying.
steps.note: On the banking app or a paper statement. Tick each one. A child with no card sits with a grown-up and finds three of the grown-up's payments on the list. Anything you do not recognise, ask the bank about it.

steps.test: Write down all the money that comes in and all the money that goes out, for seven days in a row.
steps.note: Pocket money and what it was spent on; or wages, bills, shopping and every coffee. If you did one day in Money and value, this is the same, for a whole week. A page in a notebook is enough.

steps.test: Sort that week's spending into three lists: needed, wanted, and did not notice spending.
steps.note: The third list is the interesting one: the snack on the way home, the app, the small things that added up. No judging, just sorting.

steps.test: Put a fixed amount of spending money in an envelope or pot for one week, and make it last to the end of the week.
steps.note: A child uses their pocket money. A grown-up uses a week's money for extras (coffees, snacks, treats), taken out as cash or written as a number on the envelope. If it runs out on Thursday, that is useful to know; do the week again.

steps.test: Plan one meal on paper: the ingredients, a price beside each, and a total.
steps.note: Spaghetti, a stew, a packed lunch for three days. Prices from a supermarket website or last week's receipt. Count only what you need to buy, not what is already in the cupboard.

steps.test: Shop for that meal with a budget just over your total, keeping a running total as you go, and come in under it.
steps.note: Round each item up as you put it in the basket and add it in your head or on your phone. A child does this with a grown-up and family money; the grown-up only helps if asked.

steps.test: Plan a whole week's food shop on paper, with a price beside each item and a budget at the bottom.
steps.note: Plan the meals first, then write the list from the meals, then price it. For a child, this is a week of their own packed lunches or breakfasts, worked out with a grown-up.

steps.test: Do that week's shop, come in under budget, and check the receipt against the shelf prices.
steps.note: Keep your running total, swap an item if you go over, and check the receipt before you leave the shop. A child does it with a grown-up beside them, holding the list and the total. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side

tracks.name: Earning
tracks.line: From writing down five jobs you could do to keeping three regular paying customers for twelve weeks.
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child earns only with a grown-up's say-so, only for people the family knows, and never gives their own details to strangers or online. It is about being paid for work: agreeing a job and a price before you start, doing it well, keeping a record, turning up on time, telling people what you offer, and going back to check your work. It ends with three regular customers kept for twelve weeks. Where you live there may be laws about the age and hours for working for a business, and rules about telling the tax office once you earn regularly; the notes say where to check.
tracks.who: From about eight, with a grown-up's say-so

steps.test: Write down five jobs that people near you pay to have done, which you could do this month.
steps.note: Washing a car, walking a dog, weeding a garden, carrying shopping, cleaning ground-floor windows, sorting a shed, showing somebody how to use their phone, helping a younger child with reading. A child writes jobs for family and neighbours the family already knows.

steps.test: Agree one paid job with somebody you know: exactly what will be done, by when, and for how much, before you start.
steps.note: A child agrees a job with a grown-up at home, beyond their usual chores, or with a neighbour the grown-up knows and has said yes to. A grown-up agrees one with a friend, relative or neighbour. Say it back to them: "So, all the weeds out of the front bed by Saturday, for 10."

steps.test: Do that job to the standard you agreed, tidy up after, and show the person before you are paid.
steps.note: Put tools back, sweep up, check the corners. "I have finished; would you like to look?" Being paid after they have seen it is fair to you both.

steps.test: Start an earnings page and write in it: the date, the job, who it was for, how long it took, and what you were paid.
steps.note: A page in a notebook or a note on the phone. A child uses first names only. Add every job from now on, the same day.

steps.test: Ask the person you did the job for what you could do better next time, and write it down.
steps.note: "Is there anything you would like done differently next time?" Listen without explaining. Write their exact words on the earnings page.

steps.test: Find out what people near you usually pay for one of your jobs, and set your own price for it.
steps.note: Ask two or three people what they pay for a dog walk or a car wash, or look at local noticeboards and adverts. A child sets a price with a grown-up. Write it down.

steps.test: Tell somebody what you charge for that job, as a plain number, with no apology before or after it.
steps.note: "I walk dogs for 5 an hour." Then stop talking. Practise saying it at home first. Somebody the family knows is a good first person to tell.

steps.test: Do a paid job for somebody outside your own household.
steps.note: A child works only for people the family knows, with a grown-up's say-so, and a grown-up always knows where they are; a child never goes into a house alone that the grown-up has not agreed. Agree the job and the price first, as on rung two.

steps.test: Turn up at exactly the agreed time for three jobs in a row, and send word ahead if anything has to change.
steps.note: Set a reminder the day before and an alarm to leave. If you will be late or cannot come, say so before, not after. Write the three times on your earnings page.

steps.test: Write a short note or card that says what you offer, your price, and how to reach you.
steps.note: Three lines: "Car washing, inside and out. 8 a car. Ask for Sam." A child puts a grown-up's phone number on it, never their own details. A grown-up leaves off a home address, and hand-written is fine.

steps.test: Give your note to five people you or your family know, or put it on a noticeboard where you have asked permission.
steps.note: Neighbours, a club, a place of worship, a shop or library noticeboard (ask at the counter first). A child never posts it online.

steps.test: Get one new paid job from somebody who saw your note.
steps.note: Agree it the same way as before: what, when, how much. If nobody has asked within a week, give the note to five more people.

steps.test: A week after a finished job, go back and ask whether anything needs putting right, and put it right for no charge.
steps.note: "I just wanted to check the fence paint has held up." Most of the time the answer is "it is fine". When it is not, fixing it for nothing is what makes people ask you again.

steps.test: Do the same job for the same person on a regular day, four times.
steps.note: Every Saturday morning, every Tuesday after school. Same time, same standard. Write each one on your earnings page.

steps.test: Ask a pleased customer whether there is another job they would like done.
steps.note: "While I am here, is there anything else you need doing?" Say your price for it plainly before you start.

steps.test: Work out what you really earned per hour on your last five jobs, including the time getting there and back.
steps.note: Add the pay, add all the hours including travel, divide. Write the number down. Notice which job paid best per hour; it is often not the one with the biggest payment.

steps.test: Set a higher price for new customers, and say it plainly the next time somebody asks.
steps.note: Keep the old price for people who already pay you, if you like. A child agrees the new price with a grown-up first. Some will say no; write down who says yes.

steps.test: Take on a job that needs two, bring somebody in, agree their share before you start, and pay it to them in full.
steps.note: A big garden, a garage to clear, a lot of cars at once. A child brings a friend or brother or sister, with both families' say-so. Pay them the same day.

steps.test: Put aside half of everything you earn for four weeks, towards something you have written down.
steps.note: A jar, an envelope or a separate account. Write what it is for and how much it needs at the top of the earnings page.

steps.test: Keep at least three regular paying customers for twelve weeks running, on time for every job.
steps.note: Your earnings page shows it: three names, a job each week or each fortnight, every one written down. A grown-up earning regularly on the side checks what their national tax office says about it. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Selling
tracks.line: From one sentence that says what you sell to thirty sales of the same thing, with five people who came back.
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child sells only with a grown-up beside them, to people the family knows or at an event where selling is allowed, and never online or to strangers on their own. It is about selling one thing well and honestly: saying what it is in a sentence, offering it and hearing no, asking what people want, keeping a sales page, running a table, telling a customer the truth even when it costs a sale, and changing what you sell because of what buyers say. It ends with thirty sales of the same thing, all written down, with five people who came back for more. Sell only things you made, grew, or own and have the owner's say-so to sell, and only where the rules where you live allow it.
tracks.who: From about eight, with a grown-up for every sale

steps.test: Pick one thing you could sell, and write one sentence that says what it is, who it is for, and the price.
steps.note: "Home-grown tomato plants, ready to plant out, 2 each." "Hand-painted bookmarks for readers, 1 each." A child picks something made with a grown-up: biscuits, painted stones, cards. Anything from the house needs its owner's say-so.

steps.test: Say that sentence out loud until you can say it five times in a row without looking.
steps.note: In front of a mirror, or into your phone and play it back. Can you hear what it is, who it is for and the price? If any part is unclear, change the sentence and try again.

steps.test: Offer it to one person you know, and ask plainly whether they would like one.
steps.note: Say your sentence, then "Would you like one?", then wait. A yes and a no are both answers. A child does this with a grown-up beside them.

steps.test: Offer it to three more people, and write down every yes and every no.
steps.note: Friends, neighbours, people at a club. Face to face is best. The list of no answers is as useful as the list of yes answers.

steps.test: Before you offer it to the next person, ask what they are looking for, and only offer if it fits.
steps.note: "Do you grow anything?" before the tomato plants; "Do you read much?" before the bookmarks. If it does not fit, say so and do not offer it; that is part of selling honestly.

steps.test: Start a sales page: the date, what you sold, who to (first name only), the price, and what it cost you to make or get.
steps.note: Include every cost: ingredients, pots, bags, travel. A notebook page is enough. Add every sale from now on, the same day.

steps.test: Offer it to ten people you have not offered it to before, and keep going after each no.
steps.note: Over a few days is fine. A child offers only to people the family knows, with a grown-up. A grown-up selling to strangers online meets in a busy public place for any hand-over and never shares a home address.

steps.test: After a no, ask politely what would make it right for them, and write down the answer.
steps.note: "Thank you. Can I ask what would have made it right for you?" Often it is the size, the colour, the price, or the day. Do not argue with the answer; just write it down.

steps.test: Change one thing about what you sell because of what people told you.
steps.note: A smaller size, a different colour, a pack of three, a clearer label. Write on the sales page what you changed and why.

steps.test: Sell from a table for two hours at an event where selling is allowed, starting with a float of coins and notes for change.
steps.note: A school fair, a community sale, a table at a club event; ask whoever runs it first, since selling in a street or public place often needs permission. Count the float before you start. A child under about sixteen does it with a grown-up at the table.

steps.test: After the table, count the money, take away the float, and check it matches what the sales page says.
steps.note: If it does not match, work out where the gap came from: a missed sale on the page, the wrong change given. Write down what you will do differently next time.

steps.test: Tell one customer something honest that might stop the sale: a flaw, a cheaper choice, or that it is not what they need.
steps.note: "This one has a small chip on the back." "If it is for a very small garden, the smaller plant would suit you better." People buy again from somebody who told them the truth.

steps.test: Ask a customer why they bought it, and write down their exact words.
steps.note: Right after the sale: "Can I ask what made you choose it?" Their words are often better than yours.

steps.test: Use a customer's words in the sentence you say or the label you write for your next sales.
steps.note: If a customer said "they make the kitchen smell like summer", that may belong on the label. Write the new sentence on the sales page.

steps.test: Decide what you will do if a customer is unhappy, a swap, a repair or their money back, and tell every customer that week.
steps.note: "If anything is wrong with it, bring it back and I will swap it or give your money back." Write your promise on the sales page, and keep it whenever it is asked for.

steps.test: Sell to somebody who has bought from you before.
steps.note: Tell earlier customers when you have more, face to face or through the grown-up for a child. Mark repeat customers on the sales page with a tick.

steps.test: Ask a pleased customer whether they would tell one other person about what you sell.
steps.note: "If you know anybody who would like one, I would be glad if you told them." Ask once, then thank them either way.

steps.test: Sell to twenty different people, every sale written on the sales page.
steps.note: Count the names, not the items. Over a month or two is fine. Look at which way of selling brought the most: the table, word of mouth, or asking people you know.

steps.test: Help somebody else make their first sale, and let them do all the talking.
steps.note: A friend, a younger brother or sister, a parent starting something. Help them write the one sentence, practise it with them, then stand back while they offer it.

steps.test: Reach thirty sales of the same thing, every one written down, with at least five people who came back and bought again.
steps.note: The sales page shows it: thirty lines, five names with a tick. A grown-up selling regularly checks what their national tax office says about it. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Running something
tracks.line: A plan on paper to being asked back.

steps.test: Imagine you are putting on a games afternoon for six children. Write down five things you would have to sort out before the day.
steps.note: There is no right list. A room, a start time, a helper, which games, what to drink, what happens if it rains. Anything that would go wrong if nobody thought of it counts. The point is writing it down before the day, which is most of running anything.

steps.test: Ask three people whether they would actually come.
Run one part of an outing yourself.
Make a list of everything that has to happen, in order.
Put a name against every item on that list.
steps.note: A job with no name against it does not get done. That is the whole of organising.

steps.test: Ask somebody to do one of them, and let them.
Set a date and tell people.
Work out what it costs before it starts.
Organise a small event for the group and make it happen.
Deal with one thing going wrong on the day.
Thank everybody who helped, by name.
Write down afterwards what you would change.
Run the same thing again, better.
Make an event cover its own costs with nobody topping it up.
Find out what people actually want first, then do that.
Run something where you were not the one at the front.
Hand a job to somebody who had never done it.
Cancel or change something when it was the right call.
Run something for people outside the group.
Run something people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: Making money grow
tracks.line: Saving to understanding it.

steps.test: Save for four weeks without spending any of it.
Say what you are saving for, out loud.
Put money somewhere you cannot get at it easily.
Explain what interest is, in your own words, correctly.
Work out what one coin a week becomes in a year.
Work out what it becomes in ten years with interest on top.
steps.note: This one sum has changed more lives than any other in this room.

steps.test: Save for three months without touching it.
Buy something, improve it, and sell it for more.
Do that twice and work out what you actually made.
Explain what a share in a company actually is.
Explain what a bank does with your money.
Say what inflation does to money in a tin under the bed.
Explain the difference between a debt that pays you and one that costs you.
Track a small investment for one month and explain what happened.
Watch it go down and not sell.
Track it for six months and explain what happened.
Say what you would never put money into, and why.
Spot something that was too good to be true, and walk past it.
Set aside a fixed share of everything that comes in, every time.
Teach a younger child what saving and interest mean.

tracks.name: Negotiating
tracks.line: From writing down what each side wanted in a past deal to planning, doing and reviewing a negotiation for something that matters to you for a year or more.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers from about fourteen. This is the whole method, from start to finish: preparing, opening, moving, closing and looking back. It starts at home with "if you do this, I will do that", then picks one real negotiation and prepares for it: the other side's situation, three numbers, an opening with a reason, a practice run. Then come the moves: naming a price, asking for theirs, moving in smaller steps, asking for something back each time, pausing when it gets heated, and saying the agreement out loud. It ends with a planned negotiation for something that matters to you for a year or more, such as pay, rent, a car or a contract, written up afterwards. Honest always: never invent another offer, and never pressure anybody.

steps.test: Think of the last time you agreed a price or a plan with somebody, and write down what each of you wanted.
steps.note: Buying a used car, choosing a holiday with a friend, agreeing pocket money, a price for a job. Two lines: what you wanted, what they wanted. Every negotiation starts by knowing both.

steps.test: Agree something at home using the words "If you ..., then I ...".
steps.note: "If you dry the dishes, then I will wash and you choose the music." "If you drive there, then I will drive back." This is the shape of every fair trade: nothing given without something agreed in return.

steps.test: The next time somebody says no to something you asked, ask one question about why before you say anything else.
steps.note: "What makes it difficult?" or "What would need to be different for it to work?" The answer often shows a way to a yes. Listen to the end of the answer.

steps.test: Choose one real negotiation you will have in the next month, and write it down in one sentence.
steps.note: Selling something second-hand, a price for a job you need done, your rate for babysitting or tutoring, a change to your hours at work, a lower rent at renewal. Pick something real; the next rungs prepare you for it.

steps.test: For that negotiation, write down three things about the other side: what they need, when they need it by, and what else they could do.
steps.note: A landlord needs a reliable tenant and no empty months. A buyer may need the bike by the weekend. A tradesperson may have a quiet week. Find out by asking, reading the listing, or asking people who know them.

steps.test: Write three numbers for it: the result you would be delighted with, the one you aim for, and the one you will not go past.
steps.note: Selling a bike: delighted at 120, aiming for 100, not going under 80. If you have climbed "Being ready to say no to a deal", the last number is your limit from there. Write all three before you speak to anybody.

steps.test: Write the first number you will say, and one honest reason for it.
steps.note: "100, because it had a full service in the spring." "15 an hour, because I have first aid training." The reason must be true. A number with a reason is easier to hear and easier to say.

steps.test: Practise the conversation out loud with a friend or family member playing the other side, then swap parts.
steps.note: Give them your notes on the other side so they can play it well. Do it twice. Playing the other side shows you what they are likely to say.

steps.test: When you sell something second-hand, say your price first, with your reason.
steps.note: When you know the usual price well, saying yours first gives the talk a starting point. Say the number, give the reason, then stop and wait for their answer. A teenager selling online does this with a grown-up's say-so.

steps.test: When somebody quotes you for a job or a service, ask for their price before you give any number of your own.
steps.note: "What would you charge for that?" When you do not know the usual price well, hearing theirs first protects you from offering more than they would have asked. Write their number down.

steps.test: In a real negotiation, make each move you make smaller than the one before, and say why you are moving.
steps.note: 100, then 92, then 88. "I can come down a little because you are collecting it today." Smaller steps show honestly that you are close to your limit. Never go past your limit from rung six.

steps.test: Each time you give something in a negotiation, ask for something back.
steps.note: "I can do 90 if you can collect it tonight." "I can start earlier if the work includes the back gate." Use the words from rung two. Giving with nothing asked in return teaches the other side to keep asking.

steps.test: When a negotiation is getting tense, say so calmly and suggest a short break.
steps.note: "I think we are both getting frustrated. Can we take ten minutes, or talk again tomorrow?" Use it with a family member, a seller, or at work. A break is never a trick; come back when you said you would.

steps.test: At the end of a negotiation, say the whole agreement out loud in one or two sentences, and check the other person agrees.
steps.note: "So: 90 for the bike and the lock, you collect it Friday evening and pay cash. Is that right?" Many disagreements later come from two people remembering it differently. Saying it out loud settles that now.

steps.test: After a negotiation, write three lines: what worked, what you gave too early, and what you will say next time.
steps.note: Do it the same day while you remember the words. Keep these notes together. Before your next negotiation, read them first.

steps.test: Agree a price for your own work or time with somebody who wants it.
steps.note: Babysitting, tutoring, walking dogs, a piece of design, a garden tidy, a freelance job. Use your three numbers, your opening with a reason, and ask something back for each move. If you already charge for your work, negotiate the next job on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Ask for a pay rise or a better rate, with a written list of what you have done to earn it.
steps.note: Three to five facts: extra jobs taken on, things finished, money saved, good words from customers. Book a time to talk rather than asking in passing. A teenager can do this for pocket money tied to jobs, or for a part-time job.

steps.test: Negotiate on behalf of somebody else, with their say-so and a limit they set.
steps.note: Selling a relative's car, getting a quote for a neighbour who finds it hard, agreeing a price for a club. Agree their three numbers with them first, and never go past their limit. Tell them afterwards exactly what was said.

steps.test: Plan and do a negotiation for something that costs more than a week's food shopping, using your written plan.
steps.note: A used car, a big repair, furniture, a course fee. One page: the other side's situation, your three numbers, your opening and reason, what you can give and what you will ask back. Take the page with you.

steps.test: Plan, do and write up a negotiation for something that will matter to you for a year or more.
steps.note: Your pay, your rent, a car, a long contract, the terms of a new job. Use the one-page plan, the practice run, and the three-line review afterwards. That is the far end of this ladder.

categories.name: Beauty and buildings
categories.line: Why one street feels good and another does not. Shapes, proportion, arches, and your own town.

tracks.name: Looking at buildings
tracks.line: Noticing, then being able to say why.

steps.test: Point at a building you think is pretty and one you think is ugly, and say which is which.
Say one reason why. Any reason counts, including a feeling.
Find two buildings on the same street and say which you would rather live in, and why.
Count the windows on a building and say whether they are evenly spaced.
Look at a building at eye level and say what a person walking past actually sees.
Find a building with a front door that looks like it means it.
Find one where the top, the middle and the bottom are clearly different.
Photograph three you like and three you do not.
Find one thing the three good ones share.
Find one thing the three bad ones share.
Walk somebody round and show them the good and the bad, and have them see it too.
Write down, in your own words, five rules for what makes a building good.

tracks.name: Proportion
tracks.line: Why some shapes feel right and others do not.

steps.test: Fold a piece of string exactly in half by eye, then check it.
Look at two rectangles and say which one feels nicer to you. There is no wrong answer.
Divide a line into three equal parts by eye, then measure and see how close you got.
Draw a square by eye and check it with a ruler.
Draw a house and put the door at a size that looks right for a person.
Measure a door, a chair and a step, and say what they all have in common.
steps.note: They are all sized off a human body. Almost everything that feels right is.

steps.test: Find something around you about one and a half times as long as it is wide.
Find something twice as long as it is wide, and say which shape you prefer.
Learn what the golden ratio is, roughly, and find one thing close to it.
Draw the same window three sizes and say which suits the wall.
Look at a room and say whether the ceiling is too low, too high, or right.
Find a building where one part is clearly the wrong size, and say which.
Draw a front of a building with everything in proportion to the door.
Space five windows evenly across a drawn wall, by eye.
Change one proportion in your drawing and see the whole thing change.
Draw the same building twice, once well proportioned and once badly.
Show both to somebody and see if they pick the same one you would.
Find a good proportion in something that is not a building at all.
Lay out a page, a poster or a garden using a proportion on purpose.
Draw the front of a building where every part looks right beside every other part.

tracks.name: Shapes and geometry
tracks.line: Circles, squares, tiles and solids.

steps.test: Find a circle, a square and a triangle in the room you are in.
Draw a circle freehand that somebody else agrees is properly round.
Draw a square and check its corners against the corner of a page.
Draw a triangle with all three sides the same, using a compass.
Make a shape that tiles, and fit six of them together with no gaps.
Find out which regular shapes tile and which cannot.
Step a compass around a circle six times and have it close exactly on itself.
Cut and fold paper into a solid shape that stands up.

tracks.name: Symmetry and pattern
tracks.line: Repeats, mirrors, and why they calm a room.

steps.test: Fold paper, cut a shape, open it out, and see the two halves match.
Find three symmetrical things around you.
Find something almost symmetrical and say what spoils it.
Draw the missing half of a face or a building so both sides match.
Make a pattern that repeats six times without a mistake.
Make one that repeats by turning instead of by mirroring.
Find a repeating pattern somewhere in your town.
Find a symmetrical building and a lopsided one, and say which feels calmer.
Find a building that is symmetrical on purpose except in one place.
Design a tile of your own.
Repeat it in every direction and fix whatever does not line up.
Design a tile that still works when you repeat it in every direction.

tracks.name: Arches and columns
tracks.line: The old ways, and why they were used.

steps.test: Find an arch somewhere near you and stand underneath it.
Build an arch out of blocks that stands up on its own.
Take the middle stone out and watch what happens.
steps.note: That is the keystone. Nothing holds until it is in, and everything holds once it is.

steps.test: Point out the three parts of a column — the base, the shaft and the top.
Say in your own words why an arch holds more weight than a flat beam.
Find a round arch and a pointed one and say which is older.
Find a column, an arch and a dome all in one day.
Explain to somebody younger why old buildings were built this way.

tracks.name: The beauty of where you live
tracks.line: From three things you like the look of at your own door, to walking somebody round the ten most beautiful things near your home.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can walk it side by side. It works in a city, a town or a village. You start at your own front door, naming three things built by people that you like the look of. The rungs go from looking up above the shop fronts, to what the buildings are made of, to light, trees, corners and views, to drawing a row of buildings, and end with a walk you have planned past the ten most beautiful things near your home, taking somebody with you. Once you have learned to look, the walk you take every day becomes a better walk.

steps.test: Stand at your front door or a window and name three things made by people that you like the look of.
steps.note: A gate, a chimney, a railing, the pattern of the bricks, a neighbour's painted door, a lamp post, a row of planted trees. Say one word for why: the colour, the shape, how old it is. Any three count, however small.

steps.test: Walk one street near home, stop, and look up above the doors and shop fronts until you find one detail you had never noticed.
steps.note: A date carved in stone, a face or a flower over a window, an old painted sign, iron brackets, a pattern in the roof. Always stop walking and stand back from the road before you look up.

steps.test: On the same street, write down every material the buildings are made of.
steps.note: Brick, stone, wood, render, concrete, glass, metal, clay tiles, slate, mud or thatch. Notice which one there is most of. The materials used near you are a big part of why your place looks like itself and not like anywhere else.

steps.test: Find the best-kept building near you, and say three things its owner does to keep it that way.
steps.note: Clean windows, fresh paint, a mended gate, flowers by the door, a swept step. A small house kept well often looks better than a grand one left to go shabby.

steps.test: Find a street where the buildings share a height, a material or a line of roofs, and one where they do not, and say which you would rather stand in.
steps.note: A terrace, a row of shops, a street of houses built at the same time, then a street where every building is different. There is no wrong answer: say why you chose.

steps.test: Walk a street you know early in the morning or in the evening, and find one thing the low sun shows that midday hides.
steps.note: Carving that throws a shadow, the colour of brick turning warm, the shape of a roof against the sky. The sun is low early and late in every season and every part of the world. Go with a grown-up if you are a child and it is getting dark.

steps.test: Find a corner, step or doorway where people naturally stop or sit, and say what makes it a good place to stop.
steps.note: Shelter from the wind, a wall to lean on, sun, a view, a step at the right height, out of the way of people walking. Watch for a few minutes to check that people really do stop there.

steps.test: Find a spot where a tree, water or planting makes a street more beautiful, and picture the street without it.
steps.note: A tree in a square, a fountain, a canal or stream, window boxes, a planted roundabout. Say what would be lost: shade, colour, sound, movement, birds.

steps.test: Find the best view along a street near you, and take a photograph or make a quick sketch of it.
steps.note: A long straight street with a church, a hill or the sea at the end; a bend where the buildings slowly come into sight; a gap between two houses that shows the hills. Stand somewhere safe, off the road.

steps.test: Draw the fronts of three buildings side by side on one street, roughly, from where you stand.
steps.note: Boxes for the buildings, rectangles for the windows and doors, a line for each roof. It does not need to be good: drawing makes you see where windows line up and where they do not. A pencil and the back of an envelope are enough.

steps.test: Find a place near you that is unpleasant to stand in, and write down two small changes that would make it better.
steps.note: An underpass, a car park, a bare wall, a bus stop with no shelter. A bench, a tree, a coat of paint, a light, a planter, a mural. Small and real, not "knock it all down".

steps.test: Thank the owner of one beautiful or well-kept building or garden, in person or with a note through the door.
steps.note: "I walk past your garden every day, and it makes my morning." Owners rarely hear it. A child does this with a grown-up.

steps.test: Plan a walk of about half an hour from home that passes your ten favourite things from this ladder, and walk it once to check.
steps.note: Write the ten in order on paper or draw a rough map. Things from any rung count: a carved date, the best-kept house, the view, the good corner. Change the route if a stretch is dull or unsafe.

steps.test: Take somebody on your walk, show them your ten things and why, and ask them to add one of their own.
steps.note: Somebody at home, a friend, a visitor, a neighbour. Stop at each one and say what you see in a sentence or two. Their eleventh thing is the start of the next walk.

categories.name: The classical mind
categories.line: Logic, the big questions, the great stories, and one beautiful thing a day.

tracks.name: Spotting a bad argument
tracks.line: Telling a good argument from a loud one.

steps.test: Notice somebody changing the subject instead of answering, and say so afterwards.
Say what is wrong with "everybody does it, so it must be fine".
Say what is wrong with "he is wrong because he is an idiot".
Tell the difference between a reason and a feeling, in one argument.
Say what somebody would have to show you to change your mind.
steps.note: If nothing could change your mind, it was never an argument. It was a loyalty.

steps.test: Spot an argument that attacks the person instead of the point.
Spot one that says a small thing must lead to a disaster.
Spot one where somebody argues against a thing nobody said.
Spot three different bad arguments in a week and write down what was wrong with each.
Name five kinds of bad argument and give a real example of each.
Find a bad argument on your own side.
Say what you actually believe and what your reason is, separately.
Say back somebody else's argument so well that they agree that is it.
Then say why you still disagree.
Notice a number being used to prove something it does not prove.
Notice when something is true and irrelevant.
Point one out kindly, in the moment, without making anybody feel small.
Lose an argument on purpose because the other person was right.
Hold two possible answers open for a whole week without settling.
Teach somebody younger how to tell a good argument from a loud one.

tracks.name: Asking the good question
tracks.line: The Socratic habit, at any age.

steps.test: Ask why three times in a row about the same thing and see where you end up.
Ask somebody what a word really means, and keep going until it is clear.
Take a word like fair or brave and give an example and a non-example.
Ask a question you genuinely do not know the answer to.
Ask one that cannot be answered yes or no.
Ask a question and wait five full seconds for the answer.
steps.note: Most people fill the silence in two. The answer that was coming never arrives.

steps.test: Ask somebody how they came to think that.
Ask questions for five whole minutes without giving your own opinion once.
Ask the question everybody is avoiding.
Ask a question that helped somebody work something out themselves.
Change your own mind out loud, because of an answer somebody gave you.
Run a question with a group and keep everybody talking.

tracks.name: The big questions
tracks.line: From saying what "good" means to running a half-hour conversation on a big question where every view gets a fair hearing.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; younger children can do the first eight rungs out loud with a grown-up. It starts with old questions you can answer at the kitchen table: what good means, whether a lie is ever right, what fair is. Then you learn to give the best answer for a view you do not hold, and to read what great traditions from different parts of the world say about living well, in their own words, written down so that a follower would agree it is what they teach. It ends with you running a half-hour conversation on a big question where every person gives a reason and every view gets a fair hearing. This ladder never tells you what to believe; it helps you think clearly about what you do believe and understand people who believe otherwise.
tracks.who: From about ten; younger children with a grown-up

steps.test: Say in your own words what the word "good" means, and give one example.
steps.note: Say it to whoever is there, or to yourself. There is no right answer to find; people have argued about this for thousands of years. A child might say "good is when you help", which is a fine start: then ask "is helping always good?".

steps.test: Answer "Is it ever right to tell a lie?" with a reason, then give the best reason for the other answer.
steps.note: Ordinary cases help: keeping a surprise party secret, telling a friend you like a present you do not, saying you are fine when you are not. The second half is the skill: the best reason for the answer you did not give.

steps.test: Say what "fair" means, and give one real case where being fair is hard.
steps.note: For example: should an older and a younger child get the same pocket money? Should the hungriest person get the biggest slice? Is it fair that some people are born taller or faster? Pick one and say why it is hard.

steps.test: Answer this puzzle with a reason: if every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship?
steps.note: This is the Ship of Theseus, a puzzle written about by the Greek writer Plutarch nearly two thousand years ago. Then try: what if somebody builds a second ship from all the old planks, which one is the real ship? Both answers have good reasons.

steps.test: Say whether you are the same person you were at five years old, and what has stayed the same.
steps.note: Your body, memories, likes, name and the people who know you all come into it. For a child, "at five" can be "as a baby". A grown-up and a child can each answer and see where they differ.

steps.test: Say whether something can be beautiful if nobody ever sees it, and give a reason.
steps.note: For example a flower at the bottom of the sea, a star too far away to see, a song sung once in an empty room. Ask what "beautiful" is: something in the thing, or something in the person looking?

steps.test: Choose one big question and write down three different answers people could give, each with its best reason, without saying which one you hold.
steps.note: Questions like "What makes a life a good one?", "Do we owe anything to strangers?", "What is happiness?". Write each answer the way somebody who holds it would say it. This rung is practice for reading the traditions fairly.

steps.test: Ask an older person "What do you think makes a life a good one?" and listen to their whole answer without adding your own.
steps.note: A grandparent, a neighbour, an older colleague. Ask one follow-up question, like "When did you work that out?". Say thank you, and write down afterwards the part you most want to remember.

steps.test: Read one page from one tradition's own writings about how a person should live.
steps.note: Read the source itself, not a book about it. Some starting places: the Analects of Confucius (China), the Dhammapada (Buddhist), the Handbook of Epictetus (a Stoic, Rome), the Book of Proverbs or the Sermon on the Mount (the Bible), a short chapter of the Qur'an, the Bhagavad Gita (Hindu), the Tao Te Ching (Taoist). All of these are in libraries and free online in translation.

steps.test: Write down in a few sentences what that page teaches, in a way that somebody who follows it would say "yes, that is it".
