steps.note: What time they got up, what they ate, how they got to school or work, what they did in the evening. Let them wander off the question; that is often where the best part is. A phone call counts.

steps.test: Ask them what work they did, and what one ordinary day of that work was like.
steps.note: Not just the name of the job: what they did with their hands, who they worked with, what was hard. If they looked after a home and a family, ask about that; it was a full day of work too.

steps.test: Do one practical job for an older neighbour or relative, after asking what would help.
steps.note: Putting the bins out, carrying a heavy bag in, changing a bulb, reaching a high shelf, fetching a paper. Ask first, and do it their way. A child does jobs like these with a grown-up there, and never climbs anything.

steps.test: Visit an older person in person and stay for half an hour.
steps.note: Arrange it first so they are expecting you. Sit down, accept the cup of tea if they offer, and leave your phone in your pocket. A child visits with a grown-up.

steps.test: Ask them to show you one old photograph and tell you about it.
steps.note: Who is in it, where it was, what happened that day, who took it. If they have no photographs to hand, ask them to describe the house they grew up in, room by room.

steps.test: Ask what the place where they grew up was like when they were young, and write down three things they tell you afterwards.
steps.note: The shops, the games children played, what was built where, what things cost. Write the three things down the same day, before you forget. Keep the paper: it is the start of rung fourteen.

steps.test: Visit or phone the same person again within a week, and ask about something they told you last time.
steps.note: "You said your father kept pigeons. What happened to them?" Remembering what somebody said is one of the kindest things you can do for them.

steps.test: Ask them to teach you one thing they know how to do, and learn it from them.
steps.note: A recipe, a card game, a song, a knot, how to darn a sock, how to grow tomatoes. Older people are often asked for nothing; being asked to teach is a real gift. Do it back to them before you leave.

steps.test: Show them how to do one thing they want to do on a phone or computer, and let them press every button themselves.
steps.note: Making a video call, making the text bigger, sending a photo, setting an alarm. Keep your hands off the phone and say one step at a time. Write the steps on paper for them to keep.

steps.test: Bring them something you made or grew.
steps.note: A few biscuits, a jar of soup, a plant grown from a cutting, a drawing, a card with a letter inside. It costs nothing that matters: a drawing or a letter is as welcome as a cake. Check first whether they have any foods they cannot eat.

steps.test: Visit or phone the same person every week for four weeks, and mark each one on a calendar.
steps.note: Pick the same day and roughly the same time, so they can look forward to it. If you miss a week, ring to say so and go the next day.

steps.test: Take them out somewhere they would like to go, at their pace.
steps.note: A café, a park bench, a garden, a market, the seaside, a walk round the block. Ask where they would like to go. Check where the seats and toilets are before you set off, and bring a coat for them in case the weather turns.

steps.test: Write down one story from their life in their own words, read it back to them, and give them a copy.
steps.note: Ask them to tell one story again: how they met somebody, the day something big happened, a job they were proud of. Write it or record it on your phone, then write it out. A copy for them and one for their family is a gift that lasts.

steps.test: If they want to talk about somebody they loved who has died, ask about that person and listen for as long as they want.
steps.note: Ask "What was she like?" or "How did you meet?" Many older people rarely get to say the name of somebody they miss. Never press: if they change the subject, go with them.

steps.test: Bring one other person with you on a visit, and help the two of them get talking.
steps.note: A child, a teenager, a friend, somebody of a very different age from them. Before you arrive, tell the new person one thing to ask about, like the pigeons or the old job.

steps.test: Invite an older person who lives on their own to join you for a meal or a family gathering.
steps.note: A weekend meal, a birthday, a picnic in the park. Offer a lift or to walk with them, and say what time you will bring them home. A child invites with a grown-up, to the grown-up's home.

steps.test: Keep visiting or phoning the same person every week until you reach twelve weeks.
steps.note: Carry on from the four weeks on rung twelve and keep marking the calendar. By now you will know what they like to talk about and they will know you. If they move into care or hospital, keep going there.

tracks.name: Giving
tracks.line: From sharing what is in your hand, to twelve weeks of giving with somebody else now giving beside you.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts at home with the small things (the bigger half, somebody else's job done quietly, half an hour of your time) and moves out to a local group: finding out what they actually need, giving exactly that, and getting other people to add to it. It ends with twelve weeks of giving something every week, with at least one other person giving alongside you. Most rungs cost nothing, and where money comes in, time given counts just as well.

steps.test: Share something you are eating or using with the person nearest you, before they ask.
steps.note: Half your orange, the last biscuit, the good pen, your phone charger. Offer it first, not after they have looked at it. If you live alone, a colleague or a neighbour counts.

steps.test: When something is split, give somebody else the bigger half, or the better one, and say nothing about it.
steps.note: The bigger slice of cake, the chair by the window, the unbroken biscuit. The saying nothing is the part that counts.

steps.test: Do one job at home that is normally somebody else's, without being asked and without mentioning it.
steps.note: Empty the bin, make their bed, put their washing away, clean their shoes, make their tea before they get in. If they find out and thank you, that is fine; you did not tell them.

steps.test: Give somebody half an hour of your time when you had planned to spend it on yourself.
steps.note: Play the game they want, help with the homework, go on their walk instead of watching your programme. Put the phone away for the half hour, or it does not count.

steps.test: Give one thing you still like to somebody who will like it more.
steps.note: A book you enjoyed, a toy, a jumper, a cutting from a plant, a game. Not something you wanted rid of anyway: this rung is about letting go of something you would have kept.

steps.test: Make something small for one person and give it to them.
steps.note: A card, a drawing, a bookmark, a pot of soup, a note saying what they mean to you. Paper and a pen are enough. Finish it properly, then hand it over.

steps.test: The next time somebody gives you something, say thank you and nothing else.
steps.note: No "you should not have", no "I will pay you back", no handing something straight back. Being good at receiving makes giving easier for everybody around you, and it is harder than it sounds.

steps.test: Do one kind thing that nobody will ever find out was you.
steps.note: Clear the frost off a neighbour's car, bring in their bin, leave a thank-you note for the person who delivers the post, put a coin back in the trolley for the next person. Tell nobody, including here: just tap Done.

steps.test: Give up your turn, your seat, or the last one of something, so somebody else can have it.
steps.note: The front seat, the last slice, your go on the swing, your place in a queue for somebody in a hurry. Choose it; do not wait to be asked.

steps.test: Choose a small amount to give each week and put this week's aside in a jar or envelope.
steps.note: A child might choose a small coin from pocket money; a grown-up might choose a little more. The size does not matter; choosing it on purpose does. If money is tight, choose an hour of your time a week instead, and write that on the jar.

steps.test: Find out what one local charity or group needs most right now, by asking them.
steps.note: A food bank, an animal rescue, the hospice shop, a school, a church hall, a playgroup. Look for a "most needed" list on their website, or ring or email and ask. Write the answer down; the next rung uses it.

steps.test: Give that group exactly the thing they said they need.
steps.note: If the food bank said tinned fish and toilet roll, give those, not what you had in the cupboard. Your jar from rung ten can pay for it. No money: ask whether they need something you already have, or an hour of help.

steps.test: Give an hour of your time to that group, or another local one.
steps.note: Sorting donations, packing bags, helping at a coffee morning, walking a rescue dog. Ask what an hour could do. A child does this with a grown-up beside them.

steps.test: Ask three people to add something to a collection you are making for that group.
steps.note: A box at work, a box at school with the teacher's say-so, a message to family: "I am collecting tins for the food bank until Friday, can you add one?" Three people saying yes finishes the rung.

steps.test: Deliver the collection, then tell the people who gave what it was used for.
steps.note: Ask the group when you hand it in: "Where will this go?" Then send one message to everybody who added something. People give again when they know it arrived.

steps.test: Give something every week for four weeks running, and mark each week on a calendar.
steps.note: Money from your jar, an hour of time, a bag for the collection, a meal for a neighbour. It can be different each week. The calendar is what keeps it going.

steps.test: Invite one person to give alongside you for one week, and do it together.
steps.note: A friend, a brother or sister, a parent, a colleague. "I give something every week; do you want to do this one with me?" Show them what you do and do it side by side.

steps.test: Keep giving every week until you reach twelve weeks, with at least one other person giving alongside you by the end.
steps.note: The twelve weeks count from the start of rung sixteen, so you are already four in. The other person can be the one from the last rung, or somebody new. That is the far end of this ladder: giving is part of your week, and somebody else now does it with you.

tracks.who: For everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side

tracks.name: Your own patch
tracks.line: From choosing one small public place to keeping it cared for every week for twelve weeks, with something planted in it.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a child never picks up anything sharp or strange. You choose one small public place near home (a verge, a bus shelter, a path, the corner of a play park) and make it yours to look after. The rungs go from clearing it once, to reporting what you cannot fix, to finding out who owns it, getting permission, planting something, and bringing other people to help. It ends with twelve weeks of looking after it every week. One small place that is plainly cared for changes how a whole street feels.

steps.test: Choose one small public place you pass often, and write down that it is your patch.
steps.note: The verge at the end of your road, the bus shelter, the path to school, the bench by the river, one corner of the play park. Small enough to clear in twenty minutes, and away from fast traffic. Write its name and today's date on paper or in your phone.

steps.test: Go to your patch and write down everything that needs doing there, and one thing that is good.
steps.note: Litter, weeds through the paving, a broken sign, a blocked drain, graffiti, a bench that needs a wipe. The good thing matters too: a tree, a view, a wall somebody built well.

steps.test: Pick up every piece of litter on your patch.
steps.note: If you did the ten-minute street in Your town, this is the same job, in your own place, done again and again. Never touch needles, broken glass or anything you do not recognise: leave it and report it on rung five. Gardening gloves or a bag over your hand if you have no picker.
how: Take a bag, and gloves if you have them.
Work from one end to the other so nothing is missed.
Leave anything sharp or strange where it is and note where it is.
Children: a grown-up checks each thing before it is picked up.

steps.test: Sort what you collected into the right bins at home.
steps.note: Your local council's website usually says what goes in which bin. Rinse cans and bottles. Notice what most of it was: that tells you where it is coming from.

steps.test: Report one thing on your patch that you cannot fix yourself, to whoever is responsible.
steps.note: A broken street light, a pothole, dumped rubbish, a needle, graffiti. Your local council or government website usually takes these reports, often through an online form. Write down the date and what you reported.

steps.test: Go back a week later, clear your patch again, and write down how much had come back.
steps.note: A handful or a bag. Also check whether anything from your list on rung two has changed. This is the rung that shows you what the patch needs every week.

steps.test: Find out who owns or looks after your patch.
steps.note: Usually the council's parks or cleansing department, but it might be a housing body, a roads department for a roadside verge, a church, or a business. Ask the council by email or phone if the map does not make it clear. Write down a name and a way to reach them.

steps.test: Check whether the thing you reported has been fixed, and if not, report it again, giving the date of your first report.
steps.note: Polite and plain: "I reported this on the 3rd and it is still there." Most things get fixed on the second report.

steps.test: Do one job on your patch that is not litter.
steps.note: Wipe down the bench, sweep the leaves off the path, pull the weeds from round the bench or the sign. Nothing that needs tools or permission yet.

steps.test: Look after your patch every week for four weeks running, and mark each visit on a calendar.
steps.note: Twenty minutes a week is enough. The same day each week makes it easy to remember. In heavy rain, go the next dry day that week.

steps.test: Bring one person with you on one visit, and give them a job.
steps.note: A friend, a child, a neighbour who saw you there. Hand them the bag or the brush. Two people take half the time and it is better company.

steps.test: Ask the owner of your patch for permission to plant something there.
steps.note: Use the name from rung seven. Say what, where and when: "May I plant daffodil bulbs along the verge at the end of Main Street this autumn?" Many councils are glad to be asked. If they say no, ask what they would allow.

steps.test: With permission, plant something on your patch.
steps.note: Bulbs in autumn, wildflower seed in spring, a few plants split from a garden. Free: ask a neighbour or a gardening friend for spare bulbs or seed. Plant only what the owner agreed to.

steps.test: Tell your council the date you will do a bigger tidy with helpers, and ask whether they will collect the bags or lend equipment.
steps.note: Many councils will collect bagged litter from a clean-up if they know in advance, and some lend pickers and bags. Many places also have a national litter or clean-up charity that supports local tidies. Do this at least two weeks ahead.

steps.test: Get three other people to your patch for the tidy on the day you chose.
steps.note: Neighbours, family, a school group, people from a local group you know. Tell them the time, how long (an hour is plenty), and to bring gloves if they have them. A child invites their friends through the friends' grown-ups.

steps.test: Count the bags you filled, and tell people what the tidy did.
steps.note: A thank-you message to the helpers with a photo of the patch, and a note on a local noticeboard or community group. Say who helped; do not say who dropped it.

steps.test: Look after your patch every week for twelve weeks running, with what you planted still cared for.
steps.note: The twelve weeks count from rung ten, so you are some of the way there. Water the planting in a dry spell, clear round it, and keep your calendar. That is the far end of this ladder: one place in your town that is plainly looked after, by you.

tracks.who: For everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side

tracks.name: Welcoming
tracks.line: From going to the door when a visitor arrives, to welcoming every new person to your group for four weeks running.
tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts at your own front door (greeting a visitor, showing them where to sit, seeing them out) and then moves to a group you already belong to, where you notice the new person, tell them what nobody thinks to tell them, and remember their name the next time. It ends with you being the one who welcomes every new person to that group for four weeks. Being new is hard for almost everybody, and the person who made it easy is often remembered for years.

steps.test: The next time somebody visits your home, be the first to the door and say hello to them, by name if you know it.
steps.note: A grandparent, a friend, a neighbour, somebody coming to fix something. Open the door wide, smile, say "Hello, come in." A child goes to the door with a grown-up, and only for somebody the family is expecting. If you already do this, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Take the visitor's coat or bag, show them where to sit, and offer them a drink.
steps.note: "Can I take your coat? Sit here, it is the comfy one. Would you like tea, or a glass of water?" Water is a perfectly good offer. A child can take the coat and show the seat while a grown-up makes the drink.

steps.test: Before the next visitor comes, get the room ready: one clear seat, nothing on the floor to trip over, and a light on.
steps.note: Five minutes is enough. Move the pile off the chair, pick up the shoes by the door, open the curtains or put a lamp on. People feel expected when a seat is waiting for them.

steps.test: When the visitor leaves, walk them to the door, thank them for coming, and stay at the door until they have gone.
steps.note: "Thank you for coming, it was lovely to see you." Wave them off down the path or to the lift. The end of a visit is remembered as much as the start.

steps.test: In a group you already belong to, say hello to the next new person first and tell them your name.
steps.note: Your class, a club, a team, your work, a place of worship, a choir. "Hello, I am Sam, is it your first time?" Say it before they have had time to stand on their own. A child's group can be their class or their club.

steps.test: Tell that new person the three things they need first: where to put their things, where the toilets are, and what happens next.
steps.note: "Bags go on those hooks, the toilets are through there, and we start with a warm-up in five minutes." New people are often too shy to ask any of these. Three plain facts are a real kindness.

steps.test: Stay with a new person who is on their own for the first ten minutes or the whole break.
steps.note: Sit beside them, stand with them, show them where the drinks are. You do not need to fill every silence; being next to them is the point. If your friends are waiting, bring the new person over to them.

steps.test: Introduce the new person to one other member, with one thing the two of them share.
steps.note: "This is Priya, she has just moved here. Tom, you moved last year too." Then stay a minute while they talk. If you did introductions in Meeting people, part two, this time it is a newcomer you are bringing in.

steps.test: Tell a new person one unwritten rule of the group that nobody thinks to tell them.
steps.note: Where people usually sit, whether you bring your own cup, what everybody calls the leader, that the last ten minutes are for tidying up. To find one, think back to what you did not know on your own first day.

steps.test: The next time you see that new person, greet them by name and ask about one thing they told you.
steps.note: "Hello Priya, did you find somewhere to park in the end?" If you have forgotten their name, say so and ask again; that still counts. Being remembered is the moment a new person starts to feel part of a group.

steps.test: Welcome a new neighbour with a short written note: your name, which door is yours, and one useful thing about the area.
steps.note: Which day the bins go out, where the nearest post box or food shop is, a good place for a walk. Knock and hand it over with a hello, or put it through the door. A child does this with a grown-up. If nobody new has moved near you, welcome the newest person in your building or street.

steps.test: Write one page for newcomers to your group: the practical things, the unwritten rules, and who to ask.
steps.note: Use what you learned on the last few rungs. Keep it to one side of paper, in short lines. Show it to the person who runs the group before anybody else sees it.

steps.test: Ask the person who runs the group whether you can be the one who welcomes new people for the next four weeks.
steps.note: "I would like to look after new people when they come, if that helps." Show them your page. If the group has no leader, just tell the others you will do it.

steps.test: For four weeks, welcome every new person to the group: hello first, the page, somebody to sit with, and their name remembered the week after.
steps.note: Tick each person off on a note as you go. A week with nobody new still counts; be ready anyway. At the end of the four weeks, ask one of them what made it easier to come back.

tracks.name: Helping
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One thing carried, one thing given, one thing done before anybody asked.

steps.test: Carry one thing to the table before a meal, and one thing back after it.
Put your own plate and cup by the sink when you have finished.
Put your own shoes and coat away.
Give a pet its food, or a plant its water.
Do that every day for a week.
Fetch something for somebody when they ask.
Hold a door open for somebody.
Make something for somebody and give it to them. A drawing counts.
Help a smaller child do something they cannot do yet, without doing it for them.
Help tidy up a whole room with somebody, and stay to the end.
Say thank you to somebody who did something for you today.
Do one helpful thing before anybody asks, and do not tell them it was you.

categories.name: Focus and calm
categories.line: Stillness, attention, sleep, fasting, gratitude, doing hard things.

tracks.name: Stillness, part one
tracks.line: From two quiet minutes to a morning that begins the right way, seven days running.

steps.test: Sit still for two minutes, eyes closed, and count your breaths.
steps.note: Lose count, start again. Two minutes is longer than you think and shorter than you fear.

steps.test: Write down three things you are grateful for tonight.
steps.note: Small ones are best: the kettle, a text, the weather holding.

steps.test: Look at one beautiful thing for five full minutes.
steps.note: A tree, a painting, a face, the sky. Five minutes without looking away.

steps.test: Eat one meal with no screen, no book, no phone.
steps.note: Just the food and whoever is there. Notice how long the meal actually takes.

steps.test: Sit still for five minutes.
steps.note: Same as rung one, longer. A timer, so you are not the one watching the clock.

steps.test: Do the hard thing first tomorrow, before anything else.
steps.note: The call, the email, the task you keep moving. Decide tonight what it is.

steps.test: Thank somebody for something they did a long time ago.
steps.note: A teacher, a parent, an old friend. A message or a call. Most people never hear it.

steps.test: Read one page of something old and wise, and copy out one line.
steps.note: Marcus, the Psalms, Epictetus, a proverb book. One line, by hand, kept.

steps.test: Ten minutes of stillness.
steps.note: Sitting, breathing, nothing else. The mind will wander; bring it back, that is the exercise.

steps.test: A whole day without complaining out loud.
steps.note: Catch yourself, stop, say something else. Most people do not last until lunch the first time.

steps.test: Write one page on what a good life would be, for you.
steps.note: Not the money. The days, the people, the work, the place. By hand if you can.

steps.test: A full day without news or social media.
steps.note: Notice what you reach for instead. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done.

steps.test: Forgive one small thing and let it go.
steps.note: Nobody needs to know. Say it in your head, then stop bringing it up, even to yourself.

steps.test: Fifteen minutes of stillness, three days running.
steps.note: Same time each day works best. Morning, before the phone.

steps.test: Every day for a week, write down one thing you were given for nothing.
steps.note: Sight, a friend, the sea, a language, a joke. Seven days, seven things.

steps.test: Do something kind that nobody will ever know about.
steps.note: Not even the person. Pay for the next coffee, clear a neighbour's leaves, leave a book on a bench.

steps.test: Sit with a hard feeling for ten minutes without fixing it.
steps.note: No phone, no food, no distraction. Just notice it. It changes on its own.

steps.test: Twenty minutes of stillness.
steps.note: This is where it starts to feel like something you would miss.

steps.test: Tell one person, to their face, what you are grateful to them for.
steps.note: In person, not a message. Short. Watch what it does to them.

steps.test: Seven mornings running that begin with stillness, gratitude, and the hard thing first.
steps.note: Ten minutes still, three things written, then the hard thing. A week of it is a different life. Part two goes further in.

tracks.about: Two minutes still, then five, then twenty. Three things written down at night, one beautiful thing looked at properly, a day without complaining, a hard feeling sat with. It ends with a week of mornings that begin the right way. Nothing to buy and nothing to believe; just sitting, noticing, and the hard thing first.

tracks.name: Sitting still
tracks.line: From ten still minutes on a chair to thirty minutes every morning for thirty mornings running.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about twelve who has finished Stillness, part one, or who can already sit quietly for twenty minutes. Part one mixes stillness with gratitude and a hard thing first; this ladder is only the sitting, done for longer. It starts with how to sit so your body can stay put, then twenty minutes most days, then ways of sitting that many traditions use: feeling the breath at one spot, noticing when you are thinking, listening, and walking slowly between two sittings. It ends with thirty minutes every morning for thirty mornings running. If sitting quietly ever brings up something that feels like too much, open your eyes and stop; stopping is allowed, and talking to somebody you trust is a good next step.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about twelve, after part one

steps.test: Set a timer for ten minutes, sit on a chair with both feet flat on the floor, and stay still until it rings.
steps.note: Sit a little forward so your back holds itself up, hands resting on your thighs, eyes closed or looking at the floor. If you finished Stillness, part one, this will feel easy: do it on purpose today and count it. If you have never sat still on purpose before, start with part one instead.

steps.test: Find a way of sitting you can keep without moving, and sit that way for twenty minutes.
steps.note: Try three: a chair as in rung one, cross-legged on a firm cushion or folded blanket, or kneeling with a cushion between your heels. Pick the one where nothing hurts after twenty minutes. A sharp or growing pain means move gently; this is never about putting up with pain, and a chair with a back is fine for anybody with a bad back or knees.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes at the same time and in the same place on five days in one week.
steps.note: For example seven in the morning, on the same chair, before you look at your phone. The same time and place make it easier to begin because you do not have to decide each day. If a day is missed, add another day; the five do not have to be in a row.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes feeling your breath at one spot only, the nostrils or the belly, and go back to that spot whenever you drift.
steps.note: At the nostrils it feels like a cool touch coming in and a warmer one going out; at the belly it is a rise and fall. Do not change the breath, just feel it. Coming back a hundred times is not doing it badly; the coming back is the practice.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes, and each time you notice you are thinking, say "thinking" silently once and go back to the breath.
steps.note: This way of noting is taught in some Buddhist traditions, and anybody can use it. It does not matter what the thought was: a shopping list, an argument, a song. One quiet word, then back to the breath.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes, and when an itch or an urge to move comes, wait three breaths before you move.
steps.note: Often the itch fades in those three breaths, and sometimes it does not; either is fine, and after three breaths you may move slowly. This is only for itches and restlessness. Pain, numbness or pins and needles are a reason to shift straight away.

steps.test: Sit for twenty-five minutes.
steps.note: Same seat, same way of sitting, a timer so you are not the one watching the clock. The last five minutes are often where the wish to get up is strongest. Notice it, stay with the breath, and let the timer end it.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes listening, letting each sound come and go without naming it.
steps.note: A fridge humming, a car going past, birds, wind, somebody in the next room. You do not need a quiet place for this; the sounds are what you sit with. When you catch yourself thinking about a sound, come back to just hearing.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes somewhere with ordinary noise and people around you.
steps.note: A bench in a park, a library, a waiting room, a café with a drink. Eyes open and resting on the ground a little ahead of you works better in public. If you cannot go out, sit at home by an open window or with the radio on quietly in the next room.

steps.test: Sit for thirty minutes, once.
steps.note: Choose a time nobody will need you and tell the people you live with. Use whichever way of sitting and whichever method, breath or listening, worked best for you. If you have to move once, move slowly and carry on.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes every morning for fourteen mornings running.
steps.note: Before the phone, before breakfast if you can. If a morning is missed, sit that evening and carry on the next morning; start the count again only if two days in a row are missed. If you already sit every morning, do this fortnight on purpose and count it.

steps.test: On a morning you do not want to sit, sit for twenty minutes anyway, then write one line about how it went.
steps.note: Tired, busy, in a bad mood: those are the mornings this rung is for. The line can be as plain as "restless the whole time, still did it". This is for an ordinary reluctant morning; if you are ill or something hard has happened, rest is the right choice today.

steps.test: Walk very slowly for ten minutes, feeling each foot lift, move and touch the floor.
steps.note: Walk across a room and back, or along a hallway, about one step every two breaths, hands held loosely in front or behind you. Many traditions that sit for a long time also walk slowly like this between sittings. A garden path or a quiet yard works just as well.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes, walk slowly for ten, then sit for twenty more.
steps.note: Fifty minutes in all, with the walking in the middle so your legs get a rest without the quiet ending. Keep your eyes down and do not pick up the phone between the parts. Set the timer again for each part.

steps.test: Sit for thirty minutes every morning for seven mornings running.
steps.note: Getting up ten minutes earlier is usually the easiest way to find the extra time. Same seat and time as before. If a morning is missed, start the seven again; there is no hurry.

steps.test: Sit for forty-five minutes in one go, once.
steps.note: A free morning suits this. Water first, a toilet visit first, the timer set, the people you live with told. If you must move, move slowly once and carry on; forty-five minutes with one slow move still counts.

steps.test: Lead five minutes of quiet sitting for your family or a group: tell them how to sit, start the timer, and end it.
steps.note: Keep it simple: "Sit comfortably, feet on the floor, eyes closed or looking down. Feel your breathing. When your mind wanders, come back to the breath. I will ring when five minutes are up." A phone timer or a gentle bell. Children are welcome to join; five minutes is plenty for them.

steps.test: Sit for thirty minutes every morning for thirty mornings running.
steps.note: This is the end of the ladder. Keep a simple tick on a calendar by the seat; a missed morning can be made up that evening, but two missed in a row starts the count again. At the end, write a few lines about what, if anything, is different about your mornings.

tracks.name: Attention
tracks.line: From ten minutes on one thing to three hours on one thing, once a week, three weeks running.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about twelve: schoolwork, a job, a hobby, reading or a practical task all count as "the thing". It starts with ten minutes on one task with a timer, then a written aim, the phone in another room, and counting the times your mind wanders. Twenty-five minutes, then two of them, then forty, an hour and ninety, with the things that pull you away found and removed along the way. It ends with a three-hour stretch on one thing, once a week, three weeks running. Being able to stay with one thing is behind almost every other skill in this school.

steps.test: Pick one task, set a timer for ten minutes, and do only that task until it rings.
steps.note: Anything real: homework, an email you have been putting off, sorting a drawer, practising a tune. When your hand goes to the phone, put it back and carry on. If ten minutes on one thing is already easy for you, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Before you start, write down in one line what you will do and what finished looks like, then do it.
steps.note: For example: "Maths sheet, questions 1 to 8, checked." or "Reply to the three emails from Monday." A line on paper stops you drifting into something else, because you can see what you said you would do.

steps.test: Put your phone in a different room, then spend fifteen minutes on one task.
steps.note: Not face down on the desk: in another room, where getting it means standing up. If you need it for the task, turn off everything else on it. Notice how often you reach for where it would normally be.

steps.test: During fifteen minutes on one task, make a mark on paper every time your mind wanders, then bring it back.
steps.note: A tally mark, no judging. Twenty marks is a perfectly normal first number. The skill is not the wandering stopping; it is noticing sooner and coming back. Keep the paper to compare later.

steps.test: Work on one task for twenty-five minutes without stopping, then take a five-minute break away from any screen.
steps.note: Timer on, the one-line aim written, phone away. In the break stand up, get a drink, look out of a window. If a thought about something else comes, write it on a scrap and go back to the task.

steps.test: Turn off notifications on your phone and computer for one whole session of work.
steps.note: Most phones have a "do not disturb" or focus setting in the quick menu. Turn it back on afterwards if you want to. People who might need you urgently can usually still get through by phone call.

steps.test: Keep a "later" list beside you, and write down every urge to check something instead of checking it.
steps.note: Messages, the news, what that actor was in, the price of something. Write it down and carry on. At the end of the session, look at the list: most of it will not matter any more, and the rest takes five minutes.

steps.test: Finish three tasks today, one at a time, each one completely before you start the next.
steps.note: Small ones are fine: a form, a load of washing hung out, one piece of homework. Completely means done, checked and put away. Starting a second before the first is finished is the habit this rung is breaking.

steps.test: Do two twenty-five-minute stretches in one morning or afternoon, with a five-minute break between them.
steps.note: Same task or two different ones. In the break, do not open anything on a screen; that is what makes the second stretch hard to start.

steps.test: After three sessions, write down the three things that pulled you away most.
steps.note: Look at your tally marks and your later lists. For example: "messages", "hungry", "people talking in the kitchen". Be honest and specific.

steps.test: Remove or fix one of those three before your next session.
steps.note: Messages: phone in another room. Hungry: eat first. Noise: a different room or a quieter time of day. Tabs open: close them all before you start. Pick the easiest one to fix.

steps.test: Read something difficult for forty minutes without stopping.
steps.note: Difficult means it needs your full attention: an old novel, a history book, a manual, a long article about something you care about. Phone away, a pencil to mark what you do not understand, no looking things up until the forty minutes are over.

steps.test: Spend one hour on one task with no screen within reach.
steps.note: Work that does not need a screen: writing by hand, drawing, reading on paper, fixing something, practising an instrument, planning on paper. If your work needs a computer, turn off everything on it except the one thing you are using.

steps.test: Sit down to the same task at the same time on three days in one week.
steps.note: For example 7 to 8 in the evening on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. The same time and place mean you spend less effort getting started, because the start becomes a habit.

steps.test: Do one boring task all the way to the end in one go.
steps.note: The ironing pile, filing papers, cleaning out the car, copying notes up, a long form. Boring tasks are the best practice because nothing about them holds you there except you. Write the one-line aim first and tick it at the end.

steps.test: Work on one thing for ninety minutes, with one short break at most.
steps.note: Two forty-five-minute halves work well. Water and a snack on the desk before you start. Aim written, notifications off, later list beside you.

steps.test: Spend two hours on one thing, with a five-minute break every forty-five minutes.
steps.note: The same thing you did for ninety minutes, or a new one. Before you start, fill the water glass and write the one-line aim. In the breaks, stand up and move; do not open anything on a screen.

steps.test: Spend three hours of one morning or afternoon on one thing, with short breaks.
steps.note: One project, not one task list: a chapter, a garden bed, a piece of music, a big piece of schoolwork, a room decorated. Take a five-minute break about every forty-five minutes, away from screens.

steps.test: Tell somebody else exactly how you get yourself to concentrate, and help them try one thing from it.
steps.note: A friend, a teenager with exams, a colleague. Give them the one thing that made the most difference for you, for example the phone in another room or the later list, and ask how it went a few days later. Explaining it also shows you what you actually do.

steps.test: Set a three-hour stretch on one thing, on the same day each week, for the next three weeks, and do all three.
steps.note: For example every Saturday morning from nine to twelve. Put it in the calendar and tell the people you live with. This is the end of the ladder: three hours of real attention is enough to learn, make or finish almost anything worth doing.

tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about twelve

tracks.name: Sleep
tracks.line: From going to bed without a fight to running your own rest and fixing somebody else’s.

steps.test: Go to bed at the time you said you would, three nights running.
how: Decide the time in the morning, not at eleven at night.
Set an alarm for going to bed, not only for getting up.
Three nights, written down and ticked off.
steps.note: The hard part of bedtime is never the bed, it is stopping whatever you are doing. An alarm at the start of the evening does the deciding for you.

steps.test: Get up at the same time three days running.
how: Same time every one of the three, including any day off.
Feet on the floor and curtains open within a minute of the alarm.
Whatever time you went to bed.
steps.note: The waking time is the lever, not the bedtime. Fix when you get up and your body sorts out when you fall asleep, usually within a week.

steps.test: Get daylight on your face in the first hour of the morning, every day for a week.
how: Outside, not through a window. Ten minutes is plenty.
Even a grey morning outdoors is many times brighter than any indoor room.
Walk to the shop, stand in the garden, walk somebody to school.
steps.note: This is the strongest and cheapest thing on the whole ladder. Morning light is what sets the clock that decides when you feel sleepy fourteen hours later.

steps.test: Keep screens out of the last half hour before bed, for a week.
how: Phone on charge in another room, or at least across the room.
A book, a bath, tidying, talking, drawing — anything that is not a lit rectangle.
Seven nights.
steps.note: It is the endless scrolling more than the light: a screen never reaches the end of itself, so it never lets you stop. A book has pages that run out.

steps.test: Go to bed at your time seven nights running.
how: Same time, including at the weekend.
Start the last half hour early enough that the time is actually possible.
Seven nights, ticked off.
steps.note: A week is where this stops taking willpower. After about five nights the sleepiness starts arriving on its own, which is the whole point.

steps.test: Notice how you feel after a bad night, and say so out loud.
how: Name it plainly to somebody: short-tempered, foggy, weepy, hungry.
Do it on the day, not afterwards.
No excuses attached to it, just the fact.
steps.note: Joining up a bad night with a bad day is what makes anybody bother to fix their sleep. Children in particular have usually never been told the two are connected.

steps.test: Get up at the same time seven days running.
how: Every day, including Saturday and Sunday.
Curtains open, outside within the hour.
If you had a bad night, get up anyway — the lie-in is what keeps the cycle going.
steps.note: The weekend lie-in is what undoes most people. Two late mornings is the same as flying two time zones west and back every single week.

steps.test: Make your room properly dark and properly cool for a week.
how: Cover or turn off every little light: standby lamps, chargers, clocks.
Cooler than feels right — a window open, one fewer blanket.
A cheap blackout blind or even a towel over the curtain rail works.
steps.note: Dark and cool are the two conditions your body is actually waiting for. An hour of work on your room pays back every night for years.

steps.test: Keep screens out of the last full hour before bed, for a fortnight.
how: Phone charging in another room overnight. Buy an alarm clock if that is what it takes.
Decide what the hour is for before you need it: a book, a bath, a walk, a jigsaw.
Fourteen nights.
steps.note: Most people find the hour itself becomes the best part of the day within a fortnight, which nobody expects when they start.

steps.test: Have the same last twenty minutes every night for a fortnight.
how: Same order every night: teeth, room ready, curtains, a few pages, light off.
Boring on purpose. The sameness is the medicine.
Fourteen nights of the identical routine.
steps.note: A routine works because it stops being a decision. Children are given one and grown-ups think they have outgrown it; they have not.

steps.test: Find out how many hours you actually need, by trying it.
how: A week where you go to bed at the same time and wake without an alarm.
Write down the hours each night and how the day went.
A holiday week or a quiet week is the time to do this.
steps.note: Almost everybody guesses wrong about their own number. Knowing it means you can plan a week properly instead of hoping.

steps.test: Run your own rest for a month, and then help somebody else fix theirs.
how: A month of your own times, your own routine, nobody reminding you.
Then sit down with somebody and go through it: waking time, morning light, dark room, last half hour.
Give them the one that will help them most, not all four at once.
steps.note: One change at a time is how you help somebody. The waking time and the morning light are the two that do most of the work, so start them there.

tracks.about: Sleep is the one thing that makes every other ladder in the school easier, and it is the easiest of all of them to fix, because almost all of it comes down to a handful of habits that cost nothing: the same waking time, daylight in the morning, a dark cool room, and the last half hour away from a screen. It works the same way for a child of six and an adult of forty, which is why this ladder is written for both.

tracks.name: Doing hard things
tracks.line: From one put-off job done now to one chosen hard thing done on twenty-eight days out of thirty.
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, each with their own hard things. A hard thing here means something safe that you would rather not do but know is worth doing: a job put off, a practice you want to stop, being a beginner in front of people. It starts with one put-off job done now, then keeping going ten minutes past the point you wanted to stop, being a beginner where people can see, and getting something wrong and trying again. Then it gets longer: three days, a week of a private promise, and at the end one chosen hard thing done on twenty-eight days out of thirty. If life is already hard right now, getting through the day counts, and this ladder will still be here later.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side

steps.test: Pick one job you have been putting off that takes under ten minutes, and do it now, all the way to the end.
steps.note: A reply to a message, a drawer sorted, a form filled in, homework handed over, a plant repotted. All the way means finished and put away. If you have no put-off jobs, do the one you least want to do today, on purpose, and count it.

steps.test: The next time something you are doing stops being fun, keep going for ten more minutes, with a timer.
steps.note: Practising an instrument, a long jigsaw, weeding, reading a hard chapter, times tables. Set the timer at the moment you want to stop. Something you must not carry on with, like anything that hurts, is not what this rung is about.

steps.test: Write one big job you have been avoiding as five small steps on paper, and do the first step today.
steps.note: For example "clear the shed": empty one shelf, sort it into keep and go, take the rubbish out, and so on. For a child: "tidy my room" becomes floor, bed, desk, clothes, bin. Each step should take less than half an hour.

steps.test: Do the other four steps of that job within the next seven days.
steps.note: One a day, or two on a free day. Tick each one off on the same paper. If a step turns out to be bigger, split it again rather than stopping.

steps.test: Do something you are a beginner at while somebody else watches.
steps.note: Juggling, a song on an instrument, a cartwheel on grass, a few words of another language, a new recipe, a game with a child who is better at it than you. Laughing at how it goes is fine. If it goes well, try the next bit that is harder.

steps.test: Go to a class, club or session where you will be one of the least skilled people, and stay to the end.
steps.note: A chess club, a choir, a dance class, a climbing wall taster, a sports session, a language evening at a library. Many clubs let you try once for free. A child goes with a grown-up, and the grown-up can join in too.

steps.test: Ask somebody to explain something you feel you should already know.
steps.note: How to check the oil in a car, what a word at work means, how the heating timer works, the way a child is taught to do long division now. Say it plainly: "I have never understood this properly, could you show me?". Say thank you and try it while they are there.

steps.test: Get something wrong in front of somebody, say "I got that wrong", and do it again.
steps.note: A sum said out loud, a card trick, a word in another language, a tune, a catch. The words matter: say it simply, without a long excuse, then try again straight away. Grown-ups doing this in front of children shows them it is safe to do.

steps.test: Choose one hard thing and do it three days running.
steps.note: Ten minutes of instrument practice, a page of a difficult book, ten press-ups, ten new words, making the bed properly, tidying for ten minutes. Something safe, in your control, and small enough to do on a busy day. The same one each day.

steps.test: On a day you feel like doing nothing, do one small thing you had planned, then rest.
steps.note: A walk round the block, the washing-up, one piece of homework, a short practice. Then rest properly. This is for an ordinary low-energy day, not for illness, grief or exhaustion; on those days, looking after yourself is the right thing to do and counts.

steps.test: Choose the harder of two options on purpose once today, and write down why.
steps.note: The stairs, not the lift; cooking, not a takeaway; walking a short distance, not a lift in the car; finishing the chapter, not picking up the phone. One line: "I took the stairs because I want to be able to climb hills with my kids."

steps.test: Do one safe but uncomfortable thing outdoors on purpose: a walk in the rain, up early for a sunrise, or the steepest street near you.
steps.note: Dress for the weather and tell somebody where you are going. Not in storms, ice or dangerous heat; in a hot climate, go at dawn and carry water. A child does this with a grown-up.

steps.test: Say yes to one chance this week that makes you nervous, and go through with it.
steps.note: Reading out loud at a group, joining a game in the park, speaking up at a meeting, inviting somebody round, trying out for a team. Nervous, not unsafe: never something you have a good reason to refuse. Tell one person afterwards how it went.

steps.test: Make yourself a promise that nobody else knows about, and keep it for seven days.
steps.note: Out of bed when the alarm goes, no phone at the table, ten minutes of practice, the bed made. Write it on a card only you will see. If a day slips, carry on the next day and add a day at the end.

steps.test: Go back to something you once gave up on and do one session of it.
steps.note: An instrument in a cupboard, a half-read book, a language, drawing, a sport. Stopping before was not a failure; starting again is part of doing hard things. Keep this session short, about fifteen minutes, so there is a second one.

steps.test: Help somebody else keep going at the moment they want to stop.
steps.note: A child stuck on homework, a friend learning to drive, a colleague on a long task. Do not lecture: say what they have already done, suggest ten more minutes, or do ten minutes alongside them. Then let them decide.

steps.test: Write down one thing that used to be hard for you and is not hard now, and what made the difference.
steps.note: It might be from this ladder or from years ago: swimming a length, a phone call, getting up early, reading a whole book. Keep the paper with the card from your seven-day promise.

steps.test: Choose one hard thing and do it on at least twenty-eight of the next thirty days.
steps.note: This is the end of the ladder. The same kind of hard thing as rung nine, perhaps a bit bigger, marked on a calendar each day. Two missed days are allowed so that one bad day does not end it; if you are ill, stop the count and pick it up again when you are well.

tracks.name: Noticing the good
tracks.line: From one good thing said out loud to a daily habit you have started at somebody else's table.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a family can climb it together. It starts with saying one good thing about today out loud, then making it specific, then doing it three days running. Then it turns outwards: thanking the person at home whose work nobody mentions, and the people outside who are rarely thanked at all. A jar of good things for a week, a letter by post, thirty days, and reading the month back. It ends with you starting the same habit at somebody else's table. What you notice every day tends to become what you expect, so this is worth the one minute it takes.

steps.test: Say out loud one good thing that happened today, to whoever is in the room.
steps.note: Small is best: the bus was on time, the soup was good, a dog was glad to see you. At the tea table works well for a family. On your own, say it out loud anyway, or send it to one person as a message. If this is already part of your day, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Say today's good thing with one detail: what it was, when, and who was there.
steps.note: Not "it was a good day" but "at lunch Sam gave me half his chips without being asked". The detail is what makes you notice it and remember it. A child can be asked "what exactly?" until there is a detail.

steps.test: Say one good thing, with its detail, three days running.
steps.note: Same time each day helps: tea, bedtime, the drive home from school. If you miss a day, the three start again, with no fuss.

steps.test: Make today's good thing about a person, not a thing.
steps.note: Somebody who did something, said something, or was simply there: a teacher, a neighbour, a stranger who held a door, somebody at home. Say their name and what they did.

steps.test: Thank somebody at home for one job they do that nobody mentions.
steps.note: The bins, the washing, the packed lunches, the lifts, walking the dog, fixing the wifi. Name the job and say what it saves you: "Thanks for always doing the bins. I never have to think about Tuesday." Children can thank grown-ups and grown-ups can thank children.

steps.test: Thank somebody outside who is rarely thanked for what they do.
steps.note: The bin crew, the school crossing guard, the bus driver as you get off, the cleaner at the leisure centre, the person stacking shelves. Short and clear: "Thanks, you keep this place lovely." If you already do this, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Think of the hardest day you had this month, and find one good thing in it.
steps.note: Somebody who helped, something you learned, something that went right in the middle of it, or simply that it ended and you got through it. Write the one thing down or say it to somebody. This is not pretending the day was good; it is finding the good that was there.

steps.test: Keep a jar of good things for a week: one slip of paper from each person, every evening.
steps.note: Any clean jar, box or bowl and scraps of paper. Each evening, everybody writes one good thing from the day with the date and drops it in. Children who cannot write yet can draw it or say it for a grown-up to write. On your own, one slip a day is plenty. Do not read them yet.

steps.test: Write a thank-you letter by hand to somebody who helped you this year, and post it.
steps.note: A coach, a neighbour, a nurse, a colleague, a grandparent. Say what they did and what difference it made, in five or six sentences. A letter by post is kept in a way a message is not. A stamp costs money; if that is a problem, hand-deliver it or leave it where they will find it.

steps.test: Keep the jar going every day for thirty days.
steps.note: Same jar, same time, one slip each. If a day is missed, add it the next morning and carry on; the thirty is days with a slip, not days in a row.

steps.test: Empty the jar, read every slip out loud, and pick the three best.
steps.note: A family can take turns reading. Notice what kinds of things came up most often: people, food, being outside, something funny. Keep the three best somewhere you will see them, like the fridge door.

steps.test: Start the good-thing habit at a table where nobody was doing it before.
steps.note: Grandparents' Sunday dinner, a meal with friends, a club or team night, a break at work. Go first, keep it to one sentence, and then ask the person beside you. The end of the ladder is somebody else carrying on doing it after you have gone.

tracks.who: For everybody; a family can do it together

tracks.name: Fasting
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From a comfortable sixteen hours to thirty-six, done properly.
tracks.warn: Adults only past step five. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, underweight, still growing, on medication that needs food, or have ever had trouble with eating. Children stop at step four — going without snacks is theirs; going without meals is not.

steps.test: Go sixteen hours with nothing but water, tea or black coffee, and work a normal day inside it.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until eleven the next morning. Sleep does most of it.
No milk, no sugar, no sweeteners — they end the fast in your head even when they barely do in your body.
Do it on an ordinary working day, not a quiet one.
steps.note: You have done sixteen hours before; this rung is doing it while life carries on around you. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Drink a large glass of water with a pinch of salt in it during a fast.
how: A good pinch of ordinary salt in a pint of water, drunk over an hour.
Do it at the point in the fast where you usually start feeling flat.
Costs nothing and you already have both ingredients.
steps.note: Most of what people call hunger past about eighteen hours is thirst and salt, not food. This one trick removes most of the headaches people blame fasting for.

steps.test: Sit through one wave of hunger without eating, and time how long it lasted.
how: When it arrives, look at the clock and write the time down.
Do something with your hands until it passes, then write that time down too.
Most waves are fifteen to twenty minutes.
steps.note: Hunger comes in waves and goes again whether you eat or not. Watching one arrive and leave is the single most useful thing on this ladder, because after it you stop believing hunger is an emergency.

steps.test: Go eighteen hours, water only.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until one the next day.
Water, black tea, black coffee, herbal tea. Nothing else.
Plan what you will do at the hour it gets hard — a walk is the best answer.
steps.note: Eighteen is where sixteen stops being mostly sleep and starts being a decision. The salt water from rung two matters here.

steps.test: Take a walk in the middle of a fast rather than sitting through it.
how: Twenty minutes, outside, at the hour you would normally be eating.
Notice that the hunger is quieter while you are moving.
Any weather, any route.
steps.note: Moving while fasted feels wrong and is not. A walk is the cheapest and fastest way to send a wave of hunger away, and it fills the time the meal used to take.

steps.test: Do eighteen hours on three separate days in one week.
how: Three days, with ordinary eating in between. Not consecutive.
Same edges each time so your body knows what is coming.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Repetition is what makes this comfortable. The third one is always much easier than the first, and it is the rung where fasting stops being an event.

steps.test: Break a fast properly: a real meal, eaten slowly, not a feast.
how: Eggs, fish, meat, vegetables, butter. Something you cooked.
Eat it slowly, and stop at comfortably full rather than stuffed.
Nothing sweet as the first thing that goes in.
steps.note: Almost everybody undoes a good fast in the twenty minutes after it. How you break it matters more than how long it was.

steps.test: Go twenty hours, water only.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until three the next afternoon.
Salt in your water once during the day.
Keep busy through the early afternoon — that is the hard hour.
steps.note: Twenty hours means one proper meal in a day. That is how a great many people have eaten for most of history and it is not an extreme thing.

steps.test: Do a full day on one meal, and make that meal a proper one.
how: One plate, real food, enough of it. Not a small plate.
Eat it at the time that suits your day, and nothing else all day.
Eat until you are properly full — this is not about eating less at the meal.
steps.note: The mistake here is a small meal, which leaves you hungry and cross and convinced fasting does not suit you. One big honest plate is the rung.

steps.test: Go twenty-four hours, from one evening meal to the next.
how: Seven in the evening to seven the next evening.
Water, salt, black tea and coffee. A walk in the afternoon.
Plan the meal at the end before you start, so you are not deciding while hungry.
steps.note: Evening to evening is much easier than it sounds because you sleep through a third of it and eat on both days. You did one of these in Real food part two — this is doing it deliberately.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours on an ordinary working day, not a quiet one.
how: A normal day of work, people and demands, with nothing to eat in it.
Do not tell everybody. This is not a performance.
Water and salt, and a walk at lunchtime instead of lunch.
steps.note: Finding out that you can work, think and be civil to people on an empty stomach removes a fear most people carry all their lives.

steps.test: Notice what you actually feel when you say you are hungry, and write down three words for it.
how: Do it in the last few hours of a fast.
Bored? Tired? Cold? Sad? Thirsty? Out of habit? Be specific.
Three words, written down.
steps.note: A good half of what gets called hunger turns out to be something else with a name. Naming it is what lets you answer it properly instead of with food.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours twice in one fortnight.
how: Two full days, a week apart.
Same shape both times so you can compare them.
Write down which was easier and why.
steps.note: Twice tells you whether the first one was a fluke. For nearly everybody the second is markedly easier, which is the point of doing it.

steps.test: Go twenty-eight hours.
how: Evening meal, then through the next day, then sleep, then break it in the morning.
Salt water twice across the day.
Keep the day gentle — light work, walking, nothing heavy.
steps.note: Past twenty-four hours the hunger usually gets quieter rather than louder, which surprises everybody the first time.

steps.test: Sleep through part of a fast, and notice how you sleep.
how: Go to bed inside a fast rather than breaking it at dinner.
Write down in the morning how you slept and how you woke.
Warm room, extra blanket — you will feel the cold more.
steps.note: Some people sleep beautifully fasted and some sleep badly. Knowing which you are is worth more than any general advice about it.

steps.test: Go thirty-two hours.
how: Evening meal to the following morning, through a full day and a night.
Salt and water properly. Do not skip this — it is what keeps your head clear.
Stop if you feel genuinely unwell rather than merely uncomfortable. That is not failure, that is sense.
steps.note: Knowing the difference between uncomfortable and unwell is the real skill of this ladder. Uncomfortable you can sit through; unwell you eat.

steps.test: Do something you would normally need a meal for, while fasted.
how: A long walk, a day out with the children, a hard morning's work, a hill.
Water and salt with you.
Break the fast properly afterwards with a real meal.
steps.note: This is the rung where the point of the whole thing lands: your day stops being organised around the next meal, and that is a freedom you keep.

steps.test: Plan and cook the meal that will break your longest fast, before you start it.
how: Decide it, shop for it, and have it ready in the fridge.
Meat or fish, vegetables, butter or olive oil. Nothing sweet, nothing from a packet.
Write down the time you will eat it.
steps.note: Decisions made while hungry are bad decisions. Making this one in advance is what stops thirty-six hours ending in a takeaway.

steps.test: Go thirty-six hours, and break it with the meal you planned.
how: Evening meal, a full day, a night, and then breakfast the second morning.
Salt and water throughout, a walk each day, gentle work.
Eat slowly when you break it. Stop at comfortably full.
steps.note: Thirty-six hours done properly and broken properly is the far end of this ladder. Going further than this is a thing to do with a doctor, not with an app.

steps.test: Write down your own rules for fasting, and the ones you will not break.
how: How often, how long, and on which days of your week.
The stop rules: unwell rather than uncomfortable, ill, pregnant, on new medicine.
Who you would tell before a long one.
steps.note: The ladder ends where Real food ended: with your own written way of doing it rather than somebody else's. Rules you wrote while clear-headed are the ones that hold when you are not.

tracks.about: Real food part two took you to a sixteen-hour window and one twenty-four hour fast. This ladder is the craft of going further: what to drink, how to keep working through it, what to do when you feel rough, and — the part nearly everybody gets wrong — how to break a long fast without wrecking the good of it. It costs nothing; it is the only thing in the school that saves you money while you do it. If you are pregnant, underweight, diabetic, on medication, or have any history of disordered eating, this ladder is not for you. Talk to a doctor first.

categories.name: Creating order
categories.line: Clear it, mend it, give it away, clean the forgotten places. A life flows when the place is in order.

tracks.name: The bedroom
tracks.line: From one cleared surface to a bedroom that stays right for a fortnight.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can each do their own bedroom, side by side. The climb starts with the surfaces and the piles, takes out what does not belong, cleans and washes what does, and then turns the room into a habit: a bed made properly each morning, clothes ready the night before, a place for every thing. It ends with the room kept right for two weeks. The bedroom is where the day starts and ends, and a clear one makes both easier; renting or sharing counts exactly the same.

steps.test: Clear every surface in the bedroom and put back only what you used this week.
steps.note: Bedside table, chest of drawers, windowsill, the top of the wardrobe you can reach. Everything off, then back only what you picked up in the last seven days. The rest goes where it lives, or into one bag to decide about at the weekend.

steps.test: Deal with the chair or corner where clothes pile up, until there is nothing on it.
steps.note: Every piece gets one answer: the wash basket, a hanger, or folded into a drawer. Clothes worn once and fine to wear again go on a hook, not back on the chair. A child can do their own with a grown-up saying where things go.

steps.test: Empty the box or bag where things wait to be dealt with: bin it, give it, or find each thing a real home.
steps.note: Every house has one: the box, bag or corner where things wait. Tip it out. Each thing gets one of three answers: bin, give, or a real home. No fourth pile.

steps.test: Take out anything that is not for sleeping or dressing.
steps.note: The bedroom is for sleeping and dressing. The ironing pile, the exercise bike used as a rail, the work bag, the laptop charger: take one of them out and find it a better place tonight. If your bedroom is also where you study or work, give that one corner and keep it there.

steps.test: Clean the bedroom to a close look: under the bed, the skirting, the corners, the light switch.
steps.note: Look where you never look: under the bed with a torch, along the skirting, into the corners, and the light switch that everybody touches. A damp cloth does all of it. The phone torch is enough light.

steps.test: Wash the bedding and pillow covers, and wash the curtains or wipe down the blind.
steps.note: Check the label on the curtains before they go in the machine; if they cannot be washed, shake them out of a window and hoover them. A blind wipes clean with a damp cloth, one slat at a time. If you did the bedding this week already, do the curtains and count it. A grown-up takes curtains down, not a child on a chair.

steps.test: Make the bed properly once: bottom sheet tight, pillows shaken, covers straight and turned down.
steps.note: Pull the bottom sheet tight at all four corners so there are no wrinkles, shake the pillows and put them straight at the top, and pull the duvet or covers flat and even on both sides. Then fold the top back a hand width. Once, as well as you can, is the rung.

steps.test: Make the bed properly every morning for a week.
steps.note: The same way as the last rung, as soon as you get up, before the phone. It takes about two minutes. If you already make your bed every day, do it to the proper standard on purpose this week and count it.

steps.test: Put out tomorrow's clothes the night before, three nights running.
steps.note: Everything, down to the socks, on the chair you cleared on rung two, or on a hook. Check the weather forecast when you do it. A child can choose theirs and lay them out with a grown-up.

steps.test: Walk round the bedroom and choose a place for every thing that does not have one.
steps.note: The things that end up anywhere: chargers, hair things, the book you are reading, glasses, jewellery, the bag you use every day. Give each one a spot, like a hook, a small dish, or one drawer. A shoebox or a mug is a perfectly good home.

steps.test: Sit in the finished room for ten minutes with nothing in your hands and notice how it feels.
steps.note: No phone, no book. Sit on the bed or a chair and look round slowly. Notice what your eye goes to first and whether anything still bothers you; if something does, that is the next job, not today's.

steps.test: Keep the finished bedroom right for two weeks: surfaces clear, bed made, clothes put away, every thing in its place.
steps.note: Five minutes before bed puts back whatever the day moved. Check it each morning when you make the bed. If one day slips, put it right the next morning and carry on; the fortnight does not start again.

tracks.who: For everybody; each person does their own room

tracks.name: The desk
tracks.line: One clear surface to think at.

steps.test: Clear the desk to bare wood, wipe it, and put back the three things you use every day.
steps.note: Everything off: the pens, the mugs, the post. Wipe it with a damp cloth until it is bare. Then choose three things you actually use every day, and only those go back. A kitchen table you work at counts.

steps.test: Every loose paper into one pile, then through it once: bin, file, or act on it today.
steps.note: Gather every loose piece of paper in the house into one pile. Go through it once, top to bottom: bin it, put it in a folder, or do what it asks today. A shoebox is a perfectly good folder.

steps.test: Sort the drawers: one drawer for what you use, everything else out.
steps.note: Pick one drawer to hold what you use: pens that work, the stapler, the chargers you need. Everything else comes out of the drawers and gets a home somewhere else, or goes.

steps.test: Tame the cables: unplug what is not used, coil and label the rest.
steps.note: Unplug anything that has not been used this month. Coil the rest loosely and hold each one with a bread-bag tie or a strip of paper. Write on the tie what the cable is for.

steps.test: Put one thing on it that you are glad to look at.
Sit down and check the chair and the screen are at the right height.
steps.note: Sit as you normally do. Your feet should be flat on the floor and the top of the screen at eye level. A cushion raises you, a stack of books raises the screen. Nothing needs buying.

steps.test: Set the desk each evening for the morning: a clear surface and one thing ready. Do it for a week.
Work a whole session at the clear desk and notice the difference.

tracks.name: The wardrobe
tracks.line: Only clothes you are glad to put on.

steps.test: Take every piece of clothing out and put it on the bed. All of it.
Try on anything you are unsure about. Keep only what fits now and what you are glad to wear.
Bag the rest today: give it, sell it, or bin what is worn out.
Put back what stays so you can see every piece at once.
Mend, or take to be mended, anything kept with a button, a hem or a zip gone.
Put the out-of-season things somewhere else entirely.
steps.note: Summer things in winter, heavy coats in summer. Fold them into a bag or a box and put it under the bed, on top of the wardrobe, or in the loft. What is left is only what you can wear this month.

steps.test: Work out what you are actually missing, and write the list.
steps.note: Look at what you wear every week and ask what would make mornings easier. A plain jumper that goes with everything, a pair of shoes that do not hurt. Write the list. Buying is not today; knowing is.

steps.test: Dress for a week from the finished wardrobe and count how many mornings were quicker.

tracks.name: Broken things
tracks.line: Fix it or let it go.

steps.test: Walk the whole house with a notebook and list every broken thing.
steps.note: Room by room with a pen: the dripping tap, the door that sticks, the lamp with a dead bulb, the drawer that jams, the phone with a cracked screen. Just the list tonight. Seeing it all written down is the job.

steps.test: Fix three small things from the list today.
For each thing you will not fix, decide today: bin it, or take it to be repaired this week.
Take the ones for repair out of the house.
Fix one thing that needs a part or a tool: order the part, get the tool, do it.
Fix something you have walked past for a year.
steps.note: Every home has one thing everybody has stepped round for a year. The loose handle, the wobbly chair, the cupboard door on one hinge. Tonight, fix that one. A free video search of the exact problem usually shows how.

steps.test: Replace what has to be replaced, rather than leaving the gap.
Fix or remove the last thing on the list.
Notice one thing that broke because it was never maintained.
Do the one maintenance job that would stop it happening again.
Fix something for somebody else in the house.
Keep a page for broken things and clear it every Sunday for a month.

tracks.name: Giving away
tracks.line: What no longer serves you can serve somebody.

steps.test: Fill one bag with things you have not used in a year. Today.
steps.note: Any bag. Walk the house and fill it with things you have not used in a year: the spare mugs, the gadget in its box, the clothes that wait for a different you. Tie it and put it by the front door.

steps.test: Take it to a charity shop, a friend, or a giving box the same day.
Do the kitchen: gadgets, mugs, tins past their date. One bag out.
steps.note: Open every kitchen cupboard. The third spatula, the mugs nobody picks, the machine used twice, the tins past their date. One bag of things to give, one bin bag for what is past it.

steps.test: Do the books, games and hobby things you have finished with. Pass them on.
steps.note: Books you have read and will not read again, board games nobody asks for, the kit from a hobby you have finished with. Put them in a bag for a friend, a school, or a charity shop.

steps.test: Do the bathroom cupboard and the medicine box.
steps.note: Take everything out of the bathroom cupboard. Check every date on the medicines. Out-of-date medicines go back to a pharmacy, not in the bin. Half-used bottles you do not like: out.

steps.test: Do the shed, the garage or the loft corner you avoid.
Give away one thing that is good and that you like, to somebody who will use it more.
steps.note: Not the thing you do not want. Something good that you like and hardly use: a book you loved, a good coat, a tool. Pick the person who will use it more and send them a message to say it is theirs.

steps.test: Ask each person in the house to fill one bag too.
Sell one thing rather than keeping it "just in case".
Let go of one thing you kept only because it cost money.
Keep the bag by the door and add to it for a fortnight.
A month on, count what you missed.

tracks.name: The phone and the inbox
tracks.line: The clutter you carry in your pocket.

steps.test: Delete every app you have not opened in a month.
steps.note: Go through your apps page by page. If you cannot remember opening it in the last month, delete it. You can always get it back for free. Most phones can list apps by last use in the settings.

steps.test: Delete the screenshots and the junk photos from the last month.
steps.note: Open your photos and scroll back one month. Delete the screenshots you no longer need, the blurry ones, the six copies of the same thing. Keep the best one of each.

steps.test: Unsubscribe from twenty emails you never read.
steps.note: Open your email and search the word unsubscribe. For every newsletter or shop email you never read, open one and press the unsubscribe link at the bottom. Count to twenty.

steps.test: Turn off every notification that is not a person talking to you.
steps.note: Settings, then notifications. Go down the list. Messages and calls from people stay on. Shops, games, news and anything else that buzzes you: off. You can still open the app whenever you choose.

steps.test: Get the inbox to empty once: archive, delete, or act.
steps.note: Start with the oldest. Anything older than a month that needs nothing from you: archive it all at once. Then go through what is left: reply, delete, or archive. The goal is an empty inbox once, tonight.

steps.test: Clear the home screen to one page of what you use.
steps.note: Keep only the apps you use every day on the first page, eight or so. Everything else goes onto the second page or into one folder. The first page is what your thumb sees first.

steps.test: Put the two apps that eat the most time off the first page.
Back up the photographs you would be sick to lose.
steps.note: The photographs you would be most sorry to lose: children, weddings, the people who are gone. Turn on your phone's free photo backup, or copy them onto a computer or a memory stick you already own.
