extra.note: Rinse and dry what you use first. A cereal box cut down makes a drawer divider; a tin with smooth edges makes a pen pot. Use tape, string or glue you already have, and cover it with old paper if you like. Put it to use tonight.

extra.test: Draw a four-box comic strip of something that really happened to you this week.
extra.note: Fold a page into four and draw one moment in each box. Stick figures are fine; the story is what counts. Add one line of speech in at least two of the boxes. Show it to somebody, or keep it in a drawer to find later.

extra.test: Fold one paper crane, or another origami animal, by following one free video from start to finish.
extra.note: Any square of paper works: cut a square from printer paper or an old envelope. Pause the video after every fold. If the first one goes wrong, the second one almost always goes better, so fold it twice if there is time. Put the finished one where you will see it tomorrow.

extra.test: Write new words for one verse of a song you already know, about something in your own day.
extra.note: Keep the tune and the number of beats in each line. A nursery song, a hymn or a pop song all work. Your words could be about the dog, the drive to school or the weather today. Sing it once out loud, alone or to somebody at home.

extra.test: Take ten photographs of one ordinary object, each from a different angle or light, and keep the best one.
extra.note: Try from above, from the floor, very close, by the window, and with a lamp to one side. A spoon, an apple or a shoe is plenty. Delete the other nine when you have picked, so the phone does not fill up. Make the one you keep the lock screen for a day if you like it.

extra.test: Make an eight-page little book from one sheet of paper, and fill every page.
extra.note: Fold a sheet into eight, make one cut in the middle, and fold it into a book: one short video shows how. Fill it with anything: a short story, a guide to your house for a visitor, or eight drawings. Give it a title on the front.

extra.test: Choose one place you love to visit outside your own town, and read about its history until you can tell three facts about it.
extra.note: It could be a beach, a castle, a forest park or a church you like. Look for when it was built or named, who lived or worked there, and one thing that changed. Write the three facts down, and say them out loud the next time you are there.

extra.test: Learn a poem of at least twelve lines by heart and say it out loud with the page turned over.
extra.note: Pick one from a book on your shelf or a free poetry website. Learn it four lines at a time, saying each group out loud five times before you add the next. Short cheerful poems work well for children. If you stumble, look once, then start that verse again.

extra.test: Learn the rules of the board game go with a free app, and play one whole small game on a nine-by-nine board.
extra.note: Most free go apps have a short lesson and a computer player on its easiest setting. The rules fit on one page: place a stone, surround the other colour, count the space you hold. Losing the first game is normal. If you prefer, learn draughts or backgammon the same way.

extra.test: Find out why there is no biggest prime number, and explain the idea out loud without looking at your notes.
extra.note: A prime is a number only two numbers go into: itself and one, like 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. Read or watch one simple explanation of the proof, which is over two thousand years old. Try it with small numbers on paper: multiply 2, 3 and 5, add one, and see what you get.

extra.test: Find out the history of one ordinary thing on your table, like the pencil, the fork or the teabag, and tell it in five sentences.
extra.note: Look for where it was first made, what people used before it, and how it came to look the way it does. Write your five sentences down and say them out loud. If you are at tea with somebody, ask them to guess the answers first.

extra.test: Learn the Morse code for every letter of your name, then tap your name on the table from memory.
extra.note: A free Morse chart online is all you need. A dot is a short tap and a dash is a long one, with a pause between letters. Learn one letter at a time, then tap the whole name three times without looking. If somebody else is in, tap theirs too.

extra.test: Choose one famous painting, look at it for five full minutes, then read how and when it was made.
extra.note: Open a large picture of it on a screen or in a book. Before you read anything, write down three things you notice. Then read about the painter, the year, and what the painting shows. Look again and find one thing you did not see the first time.

extra.test: Learn the names and places of the countries around one sea you have never studied, and draw them from memory.
extra.note: The Baltic Sea or the Black Sea are good choices. Look at a map for five minutes, then close it and draw the sea and the countries round it. Check, fix what you got wrong, and draw it once more. Paper and pencil is all it takes.

extra.test: Take every jar and packet off the spice shelf, check the dates, and put them back in order from A to Z.
extra.note: Bin anything well past its date or with no smell left. Tip half-empty packets into a spare clean jar if you have one, and write the name on a piece of tape. Put the ones you use most at the front. You are finished when you have being able to find the cumin in one look.

extra.test: Take every jar and bottle out of the fridge door, check each one's date and when it was opened, and put back only what is still good.
extra.note: Many jars say on the label how many weeks they keep once opened. Wipe each jar and the door shelves before they go back. Put the tallest bottles on the bottom shelf and the small jars on top. You are finished when you have a door where every jar is one you will use.

extra.test: Empty the car glovebox and door pockets, and put back only what belongs in a car.
extra.note: A good car set is the manual, a pen, a cloth, a torch, a phone cable and a copy of the breakdown number. Check the torch works. Bin the old receipts and bring the rest into the house. If there is no car, do the same with the bag you keep by the door for going out.

extra.test: Read the date on every medicine and plaster box in the house, and write a list of what you have and when each one runs out.
extra.note: Keep the list on a sheet taped inside the cupboard door or in your phone. Anything past its date can go back to a chemist, who will take it for safe disposal. Add to the list anything you would want in the middle of the night, like plasters or a thermometer. Keep every medicine up high, away from children.

extra.test: Tip out the drawer of chargers and cables, match each one to the thing it charges, and label or let go of the rest.
extra.note: Test each cable with the phone, the torch or the speaker it belongs to. A strip of tape with a name written on it makes a label. Coil each one loosely and hold it with a hair tie or a twist tie. Cables that match nothing in the house can go to an electrical recycling point.

extra.test: Open your photo backup and find one photograph from three years ago, to prove the backup really works.
extra.note: If you back up to a cloud account, sign in on a different device or the website and look there. If you back up to a drive, plug it in and open the picture. If you cannot find it, you now know what to fix, and that counts as done for tonight. Write down where the backup lives so somebody else at home could find it too.

extra.test: Clear the hall shelf or table by the front door, and put back only keys, one bowl, and what goes out with you tomorrow.
extra.note: Post goes to where post is dealt with, and everything else goes back to its own room. A bowl or a small dish for keys means they are always in one place. If the shed shelf is the bigger job at your house, do that instead with the same rule: only what is used there stays.
